[[Category:Festivals in Japan]] [[Category:Annual Events in Japan]] [[Category:Shinto Ceremonies]] [[Category:Buddhist Events]] [[Category:Winter Seasonal Words]] [[Category:November]] [[Category:dd]] [[Category:bump]] [[Category:dd]][[Category:Tori-no-Ichi]][[Category:dd]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ Unlinked]][[category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:bump 1-20 (2)]] [[Category:Temple and Shrine Authorities forks]] [[ja:酉の市]]

[[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|{{ill|Torinoichi|en]][[ja:酉の市]] at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en]][[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]]]] '''Torinoichi''' (酉の市) is a festival held annually on the {{ill|Day of the Rooster|en]][[ja:酉]] in {{ill|November|en]][[ja:11月]]<ref>See {{anchor|List of "Days of the Rooster" in November|"Days of the Rooster" list]].</ref>. It is also known as the '''Festival of the Rooster''' (酉の祭, Tori no Machi), '''Ōtori Festival''' (大酉祭, Ōtori Matsuri), or simply '''Otorisama''' (お酉様).
==Overview== [[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes at the {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en]][[ja:花園神社]] in {{ill|Shinjuku|en]][[ja:新宿区]], {{ill|Tokyo|en]][[ja:東京都]], during the "酉の市" (Cock Festival).]] [[File:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|{{ill|Utagawa Hiroshige|en]][[ja:歌川広重]]'s ''{{ill|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|en]][[ja:名所江戸百景]],'' depicting the bustling visitors heading to {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en]][[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] viewed from a brothel room in {{ill|Yoshiwara red-light district|en]][[ja:吉原遊廓]].<ref>The image echoes this scene with a hairpin in the bottom left shaped like a {{ill|good-luck rake|en]][[ja:熊手]], decorated with suggestive elements such as {{ill|Okame|en]][[ja:おかめ]] and matsutake mushrooms.</ref>]] [[File:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes during the "酉の市" at the subsidiary shrine {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Fuchū)|en]][[ja:大國魂神社]].]]
The "酉の市" (Cock Festival) is an annual event associated with shrines and temples linked to roosters or birds, such as {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|en]][[ja:鷲神社]], "酉の寺," and {{ill|Ōtori taisha|en]][[ja:大鳥神社]]. Predominantly celebrated in the Kanto region, the festival is famous for its vibrant atmosphere, with many stalls selling {{ill|good-luck rakes|en]][[ja:熊手]] amidst vigorous hand-clapping rituals. It is a well-known year-end tradition.
At {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|en]][[ja:鷲神社]], which enshrines {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en]][[ja:ヤマトタケル]], the deity is venerated as a patron of lasting military fortune, prosperity, and success in business. In the Kanto region, {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en]][[ja:鷲宮神社]] (in {{ill|Kuki|en]][[ja:久喜市]], {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|en]][[ja:埼玉県]]) is regarded as the main shrine of Ōtori Shrines.<ref>In the {{ill|Kansai region|en]][[ja:近畿地方]], {{ill|Ōtori Grand Shrine|en]][[ja:大鳥大社]] (in {{ill|Sakai|en]][[ja:堺市]], {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en]][[ja:大阪府]]) is considered the main shrine (M. Okada, "Guide to Famous Shrines Nationwide," published by Tokyo Daijingu). The connection between Ōtori shrines across Kanto remains unclear.</ref> The enshrined deities are {{ill|Ame-no-Hohi|en]][[ja:天穂日命]], {{ill|Takehi-Nateru|en]][[ja:武夷鳥命|fr]], and {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en]][[ja:大己貴命]]. Legend states that {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en]][[ja:ヤマトタケル]] prayed for victory at the shrine during his eastern campaign. Over time, faith in "酉の日精進" (ritual abstinence on the Cock Day) spread, leading to the "大酉祭" (Great Cock Festival) held on the first Cock Day of December.
In the {{ill|Edo period|en]][[ja:江戸時代]], the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|en]][[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]] in {{ill|Hanahata Village|en]][[ja:花畑 (足立区)]], {{ill|Musashi Province|en]][[ja:武蔵国]], became famous and was referred to as "本酉" (Main Cock). The harvest festival held by local residents around this shrine is considered the origin of the Edo Cock Festival. Currently, the shrine enshrines Yamato Takeru, who is said to have celebrated his victory at this location after returning from his campaign. During the Edo period, the shrine’s deity was identified as {{ill|Shakyamuni|en]][[ja:釈迦]], depicted riding on the back of a rooster. Historical records suggest that this festival dates back to the early 15th century during the {{ill|Ōei era|en]][[ja:応永]]. Pilgrims offered roosters to pray for good fortune, later releasing them near {{ill|Sensō-ji|en]][[ja:浅草寺]] in Asakusa after the festival ended.
By the late Edo period, the most prominent Cock Festival was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en]][[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] and "酉の寺" {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|en]][[ja:長国寺]] in Asakusa. During this time, the deity at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine was considered the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Myōken Bodhisattva|en]][[ja:妙見菩薩]], riding on the back of a rooster. In Edo, the Cock Festivals were categorized as follows: the "上酉" (Upper Cock) or "本酉" (Main Cock) at Hanahata Ōtori Shrine, the "中酉" (Middle Cock) at {{ill|Shōsen-ji|en]][[ja:勝専寺]] in Senju, and the "下酉" (Lower Cock) or "新酉" (New Cock) at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji. By the late Edo period, Cock Festivals were also held at shrines like those in Sugamo and Zōshigaya. In the Meiji era, the Cock Festival at Senju’s Shōsen-ji ceased, but many traditions from the Edo period persist to this day.
Asakusa's Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji Temple were located next to {{ill|Shin-Yoshiwara|en]][[ja:新吉原]], a prominent red-light district. On festival days, the district would open its gates, adding to the popularity and renown of this Cock Festival. Today, it remains the largest Cock Festival in Japan, attracting approximately 70,000 to 80,000 visitors annually, with around 150 rake vendors and 750 food stalls. [[ja:酉の市]]
== Historical Development == During the late Edo period, the most famous Torinoichi was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en]][[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] in {{ill|Asakusa|en]][[ja:浅草]], along with the adjacent {{ill|Chōkoku-ji (Taitō Ward)|lt=Chōkokuji|en]][[ja:長国寺 (台東区)]]. These events remain prominent, drawing crowds from all over Tokyo.
==Shrines and Temples Known for the Cock Festival== {{see also|{{ill|Ōtori Shrine|en]][[ja:鷲神社]]]] The Cock Festival, which rivals {{ill|Ebisu-kō|en]][[ja:えびす講]] as a festival wishing for business prosperity, is primarily celebrated in the {{ill|Kantō region|en]][[ja:関東地方]], where it originated. Unlike the Ebisu-kō, which is widely practiced not only in the {{ill|Keihanshin|en]][[ja:京阪神]] area but also throughout both {{ill|Eastern Japan|en]][[ja:東日本]] and {{ill|Western Japan|en]][[ja:西日本]], the Cock Festival remains more localized around the Kantō region. Since the Meiji period, however, the festival has spread to some shrines and temples in {{ill|Hamamatsu|en]][[ja:浜松市]], {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en]][[ja:静岡県]], and {{ill|Toyohashi|en]][[ja:豊橋市]], {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en]][[ja:愛知県]]. In recent years, it has even been celebrated at shrines in the {{ill|Nakamura-ku|en]][[ja:中村区]], {{ill|Nagoya|en]][[ja:名古屋市]].<ref>At Susanoo Shrine in Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, the Cock Festival is held after enshrining deities from Ōtori Shrine as subsidiary deities. Other celebrations in the city, such as those at {{ill|Shichiji Temple|en]][[ja:稲園山七寺]] (Ōsu Shichiji and Chōfukuji), are self-proclaimed Cock Festivals without clear historical connections to religious traditions.</ref>
The following are notable shrines and temples known for their Cock Festival celebrations. In addition to those listed, many other shrines in southern Kantō hold Cock Festivals (or rake markets): * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|en]][[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]] (Adachi Ward, Tokyo) — The origin site of the Edo Cock Festival * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en]][[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — One of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō, hosting Japan's largest Cock Festival, the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|en]][[ja:長国寺 (台東区)]] (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — Known as the "酉の寺" (Cock Temple) and the birthplace of the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en]][[ja:花園神社]] (Shinjuku Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the festival of a merged Ōtori Shrine and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|en]][[ja:大國魂神社]] (Fuchū City, Tokyo) — The festival is hosted by its subsidiary shrine, Ōtori Shrine, and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Nerima Ōtori Shrine|en]][[ja:練馬大鳥神社]] (Nerima Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the Cock Festival every November on Cock Days, attracting tens of thousands of visitors * {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en]][[ja:鷲宮神社]] (Kuki, Saitama Prefecture) — Considered the origin of the Great Cock Festival and hosts a smaller rake market * {{ill|Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|en]][[ja:熊野神社 (前橋市千代田町)]] (Maebashi, Gunma Prefecture) — Hosts the Maebashi Great Cock Festival, one of Maebashi's four major festivals * {{ill|Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|en]][[ja:金刀比羅大鷲神社]] (Yokohama, Kanagawa Prefecture) — Its Cock Festival is recognized as an intangible cultural property of Yokohama
Although the {{ill|Ōtori taisha|en]][[ja:大鳥神社]] in Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, is regarded as the head shrine of Ōtori faith, its "酉の日祭" (Cock Day Festival), held on the Cock Days in November,<ref>[http://www.ootoritaisha.jp/gyouji/ Ōtori Shrine official website]</ref> does not feature the rake markets or nighttime stalls typical of the Kantō region. [[ja:酉の市で知られる寺社]] ==Origin== The origin of the Cock Festival is explained differently by {{ill|Shinto|en]][[ja:神道]] and {{ill|Buddhism|en]][[ja:仏教]].
=== Shinto Explanation === According to Shinto traditions, the Cock Festival originated from markets held on the day of the Great Cock Festival (Ōtori Matsuri). The deities of Ōtori Shrine (or Washi Shrine) include {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en]][[ja:ヤマトタケル]], who prayed for victory during his eastern campaign at {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en]][[ja:鷲宮神社]]. He later celebrated his victory at the site of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|en]][[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]] in Hanahata, which also commemorates the day of Yamato Takeru’s death. On November Cock Days (or December’s first Cock Day at Washinomiya Shrine), the Great Cock Festival is held. The shrine tradition of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en]][[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] in Asakusa states that Yamato Takeru returned to give thanks on a November Cock Day and leaned his weapons against a pine tree in front of the shrine. This act led to the establishment of the Great Cock Festival and the use of decorative {{ill|rakes|en]][[ja:熊手]] as auspicious items.
=== Buddhist Explanation === In Buddhist tradition, specifically at {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|en]][[ja:長国寺 (台東区)]] in Asakusa, the Cock Festival originates from the market held during the unveiling (kaichō) of the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Washi Myōken Daibosatsu|en]][[ja:鷲妙見大菩薩]]. On a November Cock Day in 1265 (Bun’ei 2), {{ill|Nichiren|en]][[ja:日蓮]], the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|en]][[ja:日蓮宗]], was staying at the Kobayakawa household in {{ill|Kazusa Province|en]][[ja:上総国]] (present-day Mobara City, Chiba Prefecture). While praying for national peace, the morning star (Venus) shone brightly, and Washi Myōken Daibosatsu appeared riding on the back of an eagle. Since the establishment of Chōkoku-ji, the temple has held an annual market on November Cock Days, featuring the transfer of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu from Washiyama-dera. In 1771 (Meiwa 8), the statue of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu was enshrined permanently at Chōkoku-ji, where the annual Cock Festival continued.
=== Historical Practices === The festival is thought to have started as a harvest celebration by nearby farmers at the Hanahata Washi Daimyōjin shrine. Known also as the Rooster Daimyōjin, worshippers abstained from eating chicken meat, and even shrine families refrained from consuming eggs. Farmers offered live chickens as tributes, releasing them at the Asakusa Kannon Hall ({{ill|Sensō-ji|en]][[ja:浅草寺]]) after the festival.
Because the shrine was conveniently located along the Ayase River, it became a hub for people and goods transported via waterways. As a result, the Cock Day markets gradually attracted visitors from all over Edo (Tokyo). Gambling flourished at these markets until bans during the An’ei era curtailed the festivities.
Eventually, the thriving Cock Festival shifted to the Asakusa Washi Daimyōjin, which became the most prominent venue. Its proximity to {{ill|Yoshiwara|en]][[ja:吉原 (東京都)]], a famous red-light district, further contributed to its popularity. Over time, Cock Festivals spread across Edo and are now celebrated at many shrines and temples in the Kantō region.
Thus, the Cock Festival evolved from a rural agricultural market showcasing autumn harvests and farming tools into an urban celebration featuring auspicious decorative rakes symbolizing good fortune and prosperity. [[ja:酉の市の由来]]
==Customs== [[File:酉の市Torinoichi002.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The Cock Festival at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|en]][[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]]. The shrine distributes auspicious {{ill|rakes|en]][[ja:熊手]].]]
=== Rake Talismans and Decorative Rakes === On the days of the Cock Festival, stalls line up selling "decorative rakes" (engimono kumade), adorned with items such as okame masks and other symbols of good fortune. Shrines hosting the festival also distribute small bamboo {{ill|rakes|en]][[ja:熊手]], adorned with rice ears and talismans, as "rake talismans" (kumade mamori). These rakes are colloquially called "kakkome," a pun meaning to "sweep in" or "gather in" blessings. Originally, rakes and {{ill|hoes|en]][[ja:鍬]], along with other farming tools, were sold to local farmers around Washi Shrine on festival days. Over time, auspicious items such as okame masks began to be attached to the tools as complimentary gifts, evolving into today's decorative rakes.<ref>[http://www.torinoichi.jp/goriyaku/goriyaku_5.html Cock Festival Benefits]</ref>
The Cock Festival's auspicious items have included "tou no imo" (唐の芋, a type of yam) and "kogane mochi" (黄金餅, millet cakes), since the Edo period. The yam symbolized advancement and promotion due to its "head" shape, while its numerous offspring represented fertility. The millet cakes were believed to bring wealth. However, from the late Edo period, {{ill|kirizansho|en]][[ja:切り山椒]], a type of sweet confection, replaced the millet cakes as a festival item. Eating kirizansho during this cold season is said to prevent colds.<ref>[http://www.otorisama.or.jp/mame.html About the Cock Festival]</ref>
The decorative rake is the festival's iconic auspicious item, symbolizing the talons of an {{ill|eagle|en]][[ja:鷲]], which "grasp" its prey. The rake thus conveys the idea of gathering fortune or seizing prosperity. Decorative rakes are often bought through lively bargaining exchanges between rake sellers and buyers, where victorious negotiations are celebrated with exuberant {{ill|tejime|en]][[ja:手締め]] hand clapping. The size of the decorative rakes tends to grow larger every year, reflecting sellers’ strategies and buyers’ desires for increasing fortune.
=== The Third Cock Day === The "Cock Day" (Tori no Hi) is determined using the {{ill|sexagenary cycle|en]][[ja:干支]], occurring every twelve days.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/learning/elib/qa/qa_35.html |title=Is a Year with Three Cock Days More Prone to Fires? |access-date=2024-12-01 |publisher=Tokyo Fire Department]]</ref> Depending on the month’s alignment, November may have two or three Cock Days.<ref>For instance, if November 3 is the first Cock Day (Ichinotori), then November 15 will be the second (Ninotori), and November 27 the third (Sannotori). However, if November 8 is the first Cock Day, the second falls on November 20, and the next Cock Day occurs in December.</ref> The first Cock Day is called "Ichinotori," the second "Ninotori," and the third "Sannotori."
Years with three Cock Days are traditionally believed to have a higher incidence of fires, though there is no scientific basis for this claim.<ref name=":0" /> Consequently, in years with three Cock Days, greater care is taken with fire safety, especially in late December. Many rake merchants affix "Fire Safety" seals to their rakes during these years. Since three Cock Days occur approximately every other year, they are not particularly rare (see [[#List of Cock Days in November|List of Cock Days in November]]).
In Asakusa's {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en]][[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] and {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|en]][[ja:長国寺 (台東区)]], a nearby {{ill|red-light district|en]][[ja:吉原 (東京都)]] called [[:en:Yoshiwara|Yoshiwara]] contributed to a peculiar custom. It is said that wives would warn their husbands about the fire risk of the third Cock Day to prevent them from visiting Yoshiwara under the pretense of attending the festival.<ref>[http://ii-nippon.net/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AE%E7%A5%AD/891.html Japanese Festivals: Three Popular Theories]</ref>

[[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|{{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō Ward)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] during Tori-no-Ichi]] '''Tori-no-Ichi''' (酉の市) is a festival held annually on the {{ill|rooster day|en}}[[ja:酉]] in {{ill|November|en}}[[ja:11月]]<ref>See [[#List of "rooster days" in November|List of "rooster days" in November]] for details.</ref>. It is also called '''Tori-no-Machi''' (酉の祭), '''Ōtori Festival''' (大酉祭), or affectionately, '''Otorisama''' (お酉様).
== Overview ==
[[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|{{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en}}[[ja:花園神社]] (Shinjuku, Tokyo) during Tori-no-Ichi, with vendors selling auspicious rakes]] [[File:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|{{ill|Utagawa Hiroshige|en}}[[ja:歌川広重]], from the series {{ill|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|en}}[[ja:名所江戸百景]]: "Tori-no-Machi, Asakusa Rice Fields," showing visitors heading to {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō Ward)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]]]] [[File:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|Vendors selling auspicious rakes during Tori-no-Ichi at the {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|en}}[[ja:大國魂神社]] subsidiary Ōtori Shrine]]
Tori-no-Ichi is a traditional annual event held at shrines or temples associated with {{ill|Ōtori|en}}[[ja:鷲]] or {{ill|bird|en}}[[ja:鳥]], such as {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲神社]], Tori-no-Tera (temple), and Ōtori Shrines. Particularly prominent in the {{ill|Kantō region|en}}[[ja:関東地方]], it is characterized by lively markets selling {{ill|auspicious rakes|en}}[[ja:縁起熊手]] with vigorous clapping chants. These markets have become a quintessential year-end tradition.
Shrines dedicated to {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en}}[[ja:ヤマトタケル]] are central to Tori-no-Ichi, particularly the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Kuki, Saitama)|en}}[[ja:鷲宮神社]] in {{ill|Kuki|en}}[[ja:久喜市]], Saitama Prefecture, which is considered the head shrine for Ōtori Shrines in the region.<ref>In western Japan, {{ill|Ōtori Taisha|en}}[[ja:大鳥大社]] in Sakai, Osaka, is regarded as the head shrine, though its connection to Kantō shrines is unclear (Miyo Okada, "Guide to Famous Shrines Nationwide," published by Tokyo Daijingu).</ref>
The festival is deeply rooted in the Edo period, with notable associations to harvest celebrations and the worship of Yamato Takeru.
== Temples and Shrines Famous for Tori-no-Ichi ==
{{see also|Ōtori Shrine]] Though comparable to {{ill|Ebisu festivals|en}}[[ja:えびす講]], Tori-no-Ichi is mostly confined to the Kantō region, where it originated. In recent years, it has spread to places like {{ill|Hamamatsu|en}}[[ja:浜松市]] and {{ill|Nagoya|en}}[[ja:名古屋市]]. Famous locations include: * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|en}}[[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]] (Adachi, Tokyo): The origin of Edo’s Tori-no-Ichi * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō Ward)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] (Taitō, Tokyo): The largest Tori-no-Ichi in Japan * {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en}}[[ja:花園神社]] (Shinjuku, Tokyo): Known for a combined Ōtori Shrine festival * {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|en}}[[ja:大國魂神社]] (Fuchū, Tokyo): Features a subsidiary Ōtori Shrine
== Customs == [[File:酉の市Torinoichi002.jpg|thumb|right|300px|Tori-no-Ichi at Ōtori Shrine, where rakes are distributed]] === Auspicious Rakes === Auspicious rakes (縁起熊手) sold at Tori-no-Ichi are adorned with ornaments symbolizing luck, such as {{ill|Okame masks|en}}[[ja:おかめ]]. These rakes are purchased to "gather in good fortune." Originally sold with functional tools, the modern decorative rakes evolved from these practical implements.

[[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|{{ill|Torinoichi|en}}[[ja:酉の市]] at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]]]] '''Torinoichi''' (酉の市) is a festival held annually on the {{ill|Day of the Rooster|en}}[[ja:酉]] in {{ill|November|en}}[[ja:11月]]<ref>See {{anchor|List of "Days of the Rooster" in November|"Days of the Rooster" list]].</ref>. It is also known as the '''Festival of the Rooster''' (酉の祭, Tori no Machi), '''Ōtori Festival''' (大酉祭, Ōtori Matsuri), or simply '''Otorisama''' (お酉様).
==Overview== [[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes at the {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en}}[[ja:花園神社]] in {{ill|Shinjuku|en}}[[ja:新宿区]], {{ill|Tokyo|en}}[[ja:東京都]], during the "酉の市" (Cock Festival).]] [[File:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|{{ill|Utagawa Hiroshige|en}}[[ja:歌川広重]]'s ''{{ill|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|en}}[[ja:名所江戸百景]],'' depicting the bustling visitors heading to {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] viewed from a brothel room in {{ill|Yoshiwara red-light district|en}}[[ja:吉原遊廓]].<ref>The image echoes this scene with a hairpin in the bottom left shaped like a {{ill|good-luck rake|en}}[[ja:熊手]], decorated with suggestive elements such as {{ill|Okame|en}}[[ja:おかめ]] and matsutake mushrooms.</ref>]] [[File:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes during the "酉の市" at the subsidiary shrine {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Fuchū)|en}}[[ja:大國魂神社]].]]
The "酉の市" (Cock Festival) is an annual event associated with shrines and temples linked to roosters or birds, such as {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲神社]], "酉の寺," and {{ill|Ōtori taisha|en}}[[ja:大鳥神社]]. Predominantly celebrated in the Kanto region, the festival is famous for its vibrant atmosphere, with many stalls selling {{ill|good-luck rakes|en}}[[ja:熊手]] amidst vigorous hand-clapping rituals. It is a well-known year-end tradition.
At {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲神社]], which enshrines {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en}}[[ja:ヤマトタケル]], the deity is venerated as a patron of lasting military fortune, prosperity, and success in business. In the Kanto region, {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲宮神社]] (in {{ill|Kuki|en}}[[ja:久喜市]], {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|en}}[[ja:埼玉県]]) is regarded as the main shrine of Ōtori Shrines.<ref>In the {{ill|Kansai region|en}}[[ja:近畿地方]], {{ill|Ōtori Grand Shrine|en}}[[ja:大鳥大社]] (in {{ill|Sakai|en}}[[ja:堺市]], {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en}}[[ja:大阪府]]) is considered the main shrine (M. Okada, "Guide to Famous Shrines Nationwide," published by Tokyo Daijingu). The connection between Ōtori shrines across Kanto remains unclear.</ref> The enshrined deities are {{ill|Ame-no-Hohi|en}}[[ja:天穂日命]], {{ill|Takehi-Nateru|en}}[[ja:武夷鳥命|fr]], and {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en}}[[ja:大己貴命]]. Legend states that {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en}}[[ja:ヤマトタケル]] prayed for victory at the shrine during his eastern campaign. Over time, faith in "酉の日精進" (ritual abstinence on the Cock Day) spread, leading to the "大酉祭" (Great Cock Festival) held on the first Cock Day of December.
In the {{ill|Edo period|en}}[[ja:江戸時代]], the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|en}}[[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]] in {{ill|Hanahata Village|en}}[[ja:花畑 (足立区)]], {{ill|Musashi Province|en}}[[ja:武蔵国]], became famous and was referred to as "本酉" (Main Cock). The harvest festival held by local residents around this shrine is considered the origin of the Edo Cock Festival. Currently, the shrine enshrines Yamato Takeru, who is said to have celebrated his victory at this location after returning from his campaign. During the Edo period, the shrine’s deity was identified as {{ill|Shakyamuni|en}}[[ja:釈迦]], depicted riding on the back of a rooster. Historical records suggest that this festival dates back to the early 15th century during the {{ill|Ōei era|en}}[[ja:応永]]. Pilgrims offered roosters to pray for good fortune, later releasing them near {{ill|Sensō-ji|en}}[[ja:浅草寺]] in Asakusa after the festival ended.
By the late Edo period, the most prominent Cock Festival was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] and "酉の寺" {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|en}}[[ja:長国寺]] in Asakusa. During this time, the deity at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine was considered the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Myōken Bodhisattva|en}}[[ja:妙見菩薩]], riding on the back of a rooster. In Edo, the Cock Festivals were categorized as follows: the "上酉" (Upper Cock) or "本酉" (Main Cock) at Hanahata Ōtori Shrine, the "中酉" (Middle Cock) at {{ill|Shōsen-ji|en}}[[ja:勝専寺]] in Senju, and the "下酉" (Lower Cock) or "新酉" (New Cock) at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji. By the late Edo period, Cock Festivals were also held at shrines like those in Sugamo and Zōshigaya. In the Meiji era, the Cock Festival at Senju’s Shōsen-ji ceased, but many traditions from the Edo period persist to this day.
Asakusa's Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji Temple were located next to {{ill|Shin-Yoshiwara|en}}[[ja:新吉原]], a prominent red-light district. On festival days, the district would open its gates, adding to the popularity and renown of this Cock Festival. Today, it remains the largest Cock Festival in Japan, attracting approximately 70,000 to 80,000 visitors annually, with around 150 rake vendors and 750 food stalls. [[ja:酉の市]]
== Historical Development == During the late Edo period, the most famous Torinoichi was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] in {{ill|Asakusa|en}}[[ja:浅草]], along with the adjacent {{ill|Chōkoku-ji (Taitō Ward)|lt=Chōkokuji|en}}[[ja:長国寺 (台東区)]]. These events remain prominent, drawing crowds from all over Tokyo.
==Shrines and Temples Known for the Cock Festival== {{see also|{{ill|Ōtori Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲神社]]]] The Cock Festival, which rivals {{ill|Ebisu-kō|en}}[[ja:えびす講]] as a festival wishing for business prosperity, is primarily celebrated in the {{ill|Kantō region|en}}[[ja:関東地方]], where it originated. Unlike the Ebisu-kō, which is widely practiced not only in the {{ill|Keihanshin|en}}[[ja:京阪神]] area but also throughout both {{ill|Eastern Japan|en}}[[ja:東日本]] and {{ill|Western Japan|en}}[[ja:西日本]], the Cock Festival remains more localized around the Kantō region. Since the Meiji period, however, the festival has spread to some shrines and temples in {{ill|Hamamatsu|en}}[[ja:浜松市]], {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en}}[[ja:静岡県]], and {{ill|Toyohashi|en}}[[ja:豊橋市]], {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en}}[[ja:愛知県]]. In recent years, it has even been celebrated at shrines in the {{ill|Nakamura-ku|en}}[[ja:中村区]], {{ill|Nagoya|en}}[[ja:名古屋市]].<ref>At Susanoo Shrine in Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, the Cock Festival is held after enshrining deities from Ōtori Shrine as subsidiary deities. Other celebrations in the city, such as those at {{ill|Shichiji Temple|en}}[[ja:稲園山七寺]] (Ōsu Shichiji and Chōfukuji), are self-proclaimed Cock Festivals without clear historical connections to religious traditions.</ref>
The following are notable shrines and temples known for their Cock Festival celebrations. In addition to those listed, many other shrines in southern Kantō hold Cock Festivals (or rake markets): * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|en}}[[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]] (Adachi Ward, Tokyo) — The origin site of the Edo Cock Festival * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — One of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō, hosting Japan's largest Cock Festival, the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|en}}[[ja:長国寺 (台東区)]] (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — Known as the "酉の寺" (Cock Temple) and the birthplace of the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en}}[[ja:花園神社]] (Shinjuku Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the festival of a merged Ōtori Shrine and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|en}}[[ja:大國魂神社]] (Fuchū City, Tokyo) — The festival is hosted by its subsidiary shrine, Ōtori Shrine, and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Nerima Ōtori Shrine|en}}[[ja:練馬大鳥神社]] (Nerima Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the Cock Festival every November on Cock Days, attracting tens of thousands of visitors * {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲宮神社]] (Kuki, Saitama Prefecture) — Considered the origin of the Great Cock Festival and hosts a smaller rake market * {{ill|Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|en}}[[ja:熊野神社 (前橋市千代田町)]] (Maebashi, Gunma Prefecture) — Hosts the Maebashi Great Cock Festival, one of Maebashi's four major festivals * {{ill|Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|en}}[[ja:金刀比羅大鷲神社]] (Yokohama, Kanagawa Prefecture) — Its Cock Festival is recognized as an intangible cultural property of Yokohama
Although the {{ill|Ōtori taisha|en}}[[ja:大鳥神社]] in Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, is regarded as the head shrine of Ōtori faith, its "酉の日祭" (Cock Day Festival), held on the Cock Days in November,<ref>[http://www.ootoritaisha.jp/gyouji/ Ōtori Shrine official website]</ref> does not feature the rake markets or nighttime stalls typical of the Kantō region. [[ja:酉の市で知られる寺社]] ==Origin== The origin of the Cock Festival is explained differently by {{ill|Shinto|en}}[[ja:神道]] and {{ill|Buddhism|en}}[[ja:仏教]].
=== Shinto Explanation === According to Shinto traditions, the Cock Festival originated from markets held on the day of the Great Cock Festival (Ōtori Matsuri). The deities of Ōtori Shrine (or Washi Shrine) include {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en}}[[ja:ヤマトタケル]], who prayed for victory during his eastern campaign at {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲宮神社]]. He later celebrated his victory at the site of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|en}}[[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]] in Hanahata, which also commemorates the day of Yamato Takeru’s death. On November Cock Days (or December’s first Cock Day at Washinomiya Shrine), the Great Cock Festival is held. The shrine tradition of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] in Asakusa states that Yamato Takeru returned to give thanks on a November Cock Day and leaned his weapons against a pine tree in front of the shrine. This act led to the establishment of the Great Cock Festival and the use of decorative {{ill|rakes|en}}[[ja:熊手]] as auspicious items.
=== Buddhist Explanation === In Buddhist tradition, specifically at {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|en}}[[ja:長国寺 (台東区)]] in Asakusa, the Cock Festival originates from the market held during the unveiling (kaichō) of the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Washi Myōken Daibosatsu|en}}[[ja:鷲妙見大菩薩]]. On a November Cock Day in 1265 (Bun’ei 2), {{ill|Nichiren|en}}[[ja:日蓮]], the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|en}}[[ja:日蓮宗]], was staying at the Kobayakawa household in {{ill|Kazusa Province|en}}[[ja:上総国]] (present-day Mobara City, Chiba Prefecture). While praying for national peace, the morning star (Venus) shone brightly, and Washi Myōken Daibosatsu appeared riding on the back of an eagle. Since the establishment of Chōkoku-ji, the temple has held an annual market on November Cock Days, featuring the transfer of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu from Washiyama-dera. In 1771 (Meiwa 8), the statue of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu was enshrined permanently at Chōkoku-ji, where the annual Cock Festival continued.
=== Historical Practices === The festival is thought to have started as a harvest celebration by nearby farmers at the Hanahata Washi Daimyōjin shrine. Known also as the Rooster Daimyōjin, worshippers abstained from eating chicken meat, and even shrine families refrained from consuming eggs. Farmers offered live chickens as tributes, releasing them at the Asakusa Kannon Hall ({{ill|Sensō-ji|en}}[[ja:浅草寺]]) after the festival.
Because the shrine was conveniently located along the Ayase River, it became a hub for people and goods transported via waterways. As a result, the Cock Day markets gradually attracted visitors from all over Edo (Tokyo). Gambling flourished at these markets until bans during the An’ei era curtailed the festivities.
Eventually, the thriving Cock Festival shifted to the Asakusa Washi Daimyōjin, which became the most prominent venue. Its proximity to {{ill|Yoshiwara|en}}[[ja:吉原 (東京都)]], a famous red-light district, further contributed to its popularity. Over time, Cock Festivals spread across Edo and are now celebrated at many shrines and temples in the Kantō region.
Thus, the Cock Festival evolved from a rural agricultural market showcasing autumn harvests and farming tools into an urban celebration featuring auspicious decorative rakes symbolizing good fortune and prosperity. [[ja:酉の市の由来]]
==Customs== [[File:酉の市Torinoichi002.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The Cock Festival at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|en}}[[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]]. The shrine distributes auspicious {{ill|rakes|en}}[[ja:熊手]].]]
=== Rake Talismans and Decorative Rakes === On the days of the Cock Festival, stalls line up selling "decorative rakes" (engimono kumade), adorned with items such as okame masks and other symbols of good fortune. Shrines hosting the festival also distribute small bamboo {{ill|rakes|en}}[[ja:熊手]], adorned with rice ears and talismans, as "rake talismans" (kumade mamori). These rakes are colloquially called "kakkome," a pun meaning to "sweep in" or "gather in" blessings. Originally, rakes and {{ill|hoes|en}}[[ja:鍬]], along with other farming tools, were sold to local farmers around Washi Shrine on festival days. Over time, auspicious items such as okame masks began to be attached to the tools as complimentary gifts, evolving into today's decorative rakes.<ref>[http://www.torinoichi.jp/goriyaku/goriyaku_5.html Cock Festival Benefits]</ref>
The Cock Festival's auspicious items have included "tou no imo" (唐の芋, a type of yam) and "kogane mochi" (黄金餅, millet cakes), since the Edo period. The yam symbolized advancement and promotion due to its "head" shape, while its numerous offspring represented fertility. The millet cakes were believed to bring wealth. However, from the late Edo period, {{ill|kirizansho|en}}[[ja:切り山椒]], a type of sweet confection, replaced the millet cakes as a festival item. Eating kirizansho during this cold season is said to prevent colds.<ref>[http://www.otorisama.or.jp/mame.html About the Cock Festival]</ref>
The decorative rake is the festival's iconic auspicious item, symbolizing the talons of an {{ill|eagle|en}}[[ja:鷲]], which "grasp" its prey. The rake thus conveys the idea of gathering fortune or seizing prosperity. Decorative rakes are often bought through lively bargaining exchanges between rake sellers and buyers, where victorious negotiations are celebrated with exuberant {{ill|tejime|en}}[[ja:手締め]] hand clapping. The size of the decorative rakes tends to grow larger every year, reflecting sellers’ strategies and buyers’ desires for increasing fortune.
=== The Third Cock Day === The "Cock Day" (Tori no Hi) is determined using the {{ill|sexagenary cycle|en}}[[ja:干支]], occurring every twelve days.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/learning/elib/qa/qa_35.html |title=Is a Year with Three Cock Days More Prone to Fires? |access-date=2024-12-01 |publisher=Tokyo Fire Department]]</ref> Depending on the month’s alignment, November may have two or three Cock Days.<ref>For instance, if November 3 is the first Cock Day (Ichinotori), then November 15 will be the second (Ninotori), and November 27 the third (Sannotori). However, if November 8 is the first Cock Day, the second falls on November 20, and the next Cock Day occurs in December.</ref> The first Cock Day is called "Ichinotori," the second "Ninotori," and the third "Sannotori."
Years with three Cock Days are traditionally believed to have a higher incidence of fires, though there is no scientific basis for this claim.<ref name=":0" /> Consequently, in years with three Cock Days, greater care is taken with fire safety, especially in late December. Many rake merchants affix "Fire Safety" seals to their rakes during these years. Since three Cock Days occur approximately every other year, they are not particularly rare (see [[#List of Cock Days in November|List of Cock Days in November]]).
In Asakusa's {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] and {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|en}}[[ja:長国寺 (台東区)]], a nearby {{ill|red-light district|en}}[[ja:吉原 (東京都)]] called [[:en:Yoshiwara|Yoshiwara]] contributed to a peculiar custom. It is said that wives would warn their husbands about the fire risk of the third Cock Day to prevent them from visiting Yoshiwara under the pretense of attending the festival.<ref>[http://ii-nippon.net/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AE%E7%A5%AD/891.html Japanese Festivals: Three Popular Theories]</ref>

{{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|日本武尊}} |Sacred Object = |Rank = |Established = Unknown |Honden = |Alias = Otorisama |Pilgrimage = {{ill|Seven Lucky Gods of Asakusa|ja|浅草名所七福神}}, {{ill|Shitamachi Eight Lucky Gods|ja|下町八福神}} |Festival = November Tori Day (Tori no Ichi) |Rituals = |Access = }} '''Ohtori Shrine''' (鷲神社), located in [[Senzoku]] 3-chome, [[Taitō Ward]], [[Tokyo]], is a {{ill|shrine|ja|神社}}. Also known by its alias, "Otorisama," it is widely recognized for its November festival, the {{ill|Tori no Ichi|ja|酉の市}}. == Deities == * {{ill|Amewakahiko|ja|天日鷲命}} * {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|日本武尊}} == History == According to legend, {{ill|Amewakahiko|ja|天日鷲神}} was enshrined in this location since ancient times. It is said that {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|日本武尊}} prayed for victory during his eastern campaign here. In reality, the shrine originated from the adjacent {{ill|Chōkoku-ji (Taitō)|ja|長国寺}}, where Ohtori was worshipped. During the mid-{{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代}}, the shrine became famous for its Tori no Ichi. In contrast to the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社}} in Adachi Ward, which was referred to as "Ōtori," this shrine came to be known as "Shintori." Following the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} movement during the early {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治}} era, it became independent from Chōkoku-ji and was renamed Ohtori Shrine. == Location == * 3-18-7 Senzoku, Taitō Ward, Tokyo == Access == === Rail === * [[Tokyo Metro]] [[Tokyo Metro Hibiya Line|Hibiya Line]] {{ill|Iriya Station (Tokyo)|ja|入谷駅}} or {{ill|Minowa Station|ja|三ノ輪駅}}, about 10 minutes on foot * {{ill|Tsukuba Express|ja|首都圏新都市鉄道つくばエクスプレス}} {{ill|Asakusa Station (Tsukuba Express)|ja|浅草駅}}, about 10 minutes on foot === Bus === * {{ill|Toei Bus|ja|都営バス}} {{ill|Toei Bus Nan-Senju Office#TO08 Route|ja|都営バス南千住営業所#都08系統（グリーンリバー）}}, stop at Senzoku * {{ill|Megurin (Taitō Ward)|ja|めぐりん (台東区)}} “North Megurin,” stop at Taitō Hospital, about 3 minutes on foot During the Tori no Ichi festival, traffic restrictions cause the bus to detour. The nearest stop changes to Senzoku 2-chome (stop 28). == Gallery == {{Gallery |align=center |width=160 |height=120 |File:Ootori jinja1.jpg|Forked tree and large rake (photo taken January 2010) |File:Ootori jinja2.jpg|Forked tree (photo taken January 2010) |File:Ootori jinja3.jpg|Kagura hall and main hall (photo taken January 2010) |File:Ootori jinja4.jpg|Main hall (photo taken January 2010) |File:Ootori jinja5.jpg|Chōzuya (photo taken January 2010) }} == Related Articles == {{Commonscat}} * {{ill|Tori no Ichi|ja|酉の市}} * {{ill|Chōkoku-ji (Taitō)|ja|長国寺}} * {{ill|Red Entertainment|ja|レッド・エンタテインメント}} - A company specializing in games, animation, and other media content. Its predecessor, Red Company, was located on land owned by the shrine.{{Cite web|url=https://game-creators.jp/media/column/131/|title=Sacred Pilgrimage - Games Edition: Asakusa Travelogue|publisher=GAME CREATORS|date=2019-10-04|accessdate=2020-01-17}} == References == {{Reflist}} == External Links == * [https://otorisama.or.jp/ Official site of Ohtori Shrine] * [http://www.asakusa-torinoichi.tokyo/ Tori no Ichi at Asakusa Ohtori Shrine] {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Shrines in Taitō]] [[Category:Yamato Takeru legends]] [[ja:鷲神社]] [[Category:Festivals in Japan]] [[Category:Annual Events in Japan]] [[Category:Shinto Ceremonies]] [[Category:Buddhist Events]] [[Category:Winter Seasonal Words]] [[Category:November]] [[Category:dd]] [[Category:bump]] [[Category:dd]][[Category:Tori-no-Ichi]][[Category:dd]] [[Category:ZZZZZZZZZ Unlinked]][[category:unsorted completion categories]] [[Category:bump 1-20 (2)]] [[Category:Temple and Shrine Authorities forks]] [[ja:酉の市]]

revision.text:
[[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|{{ill|Torinoichi|en}}[[ja:酉の市]] at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]]]] '''Torinoichi''' (酉の市) is a festival held annually on the {{ill|Day of the Rooster|en}}[[ja:酉]] in {{ill|November|en}}[[ja:11月]]<ref>See {{anchor|List of "Days of the Rooster" in November|"Days of the Rooster" list]].</ref>. It is also known as the '''Festival of the Rooster''' (酉の祭, Tori no Machi), '''Ōtori Festival''' (大酉祭, Ōtori Matsuri), or simply '''Otorisama''' (お酉様).
==Overview== [[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes at the {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en}}[[ja:花園神社]] in {{ill|Shinjuku|en}}[[ja:新宿区]], {{ill|Tokyo|en}}[[ja:東京都]], during the "酉の市" (Cock Festival).]] [[File:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|{{ill|Utagawa Hiroshige|en}}[[ja:歌川広重]]'s ''{{ill|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|en}}[[ja:名所江戸百景]],'' depicting the bustling visitors heading to {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] viewed from a brothel room in {{ill|Yoshiwara red-light district|en}}[[ja:吉原遊廓]].<ref>The image echoes this scene with a hairpin in the bottom left shaped like a {{ill|good-luck rake|en}}[[ja:熊手]], decorated with suggestive elements such as {{ill|Okame|en}}[[ja:おかめ]] and matsutake mushrooms.</ref>]] [[File:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes during the "酉の市" at the subsidiary shrine {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Fuchū)|en}}[[ja:大國魂神社]].]]
The "酉の市" (Cock Festival) is an annual event associated with shrines and temples linked to roosters or birds, such as {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲神社]], "酉の寺," and {{ill|Ōtori taisha|en}}[[ja:大鳥神社]]. Predominantly celebrated in the Kanto region, the festival is famous for its vibrant atmosphere, with many stalls selling {{ill|good-luck rakes|en}}[[ja:熊手]] amidst vigorous hand-clapping rituals. It is a well-known year-end tradition.
At {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲神社]], which enshrines {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en}}[[ja:ヤマトタケル]], the deity is venerated as a patron of lasting military fortune, prosperity, and success in business. In the Kanto region, {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲宮神社]] (in {{ill|Kuki|en}}[[ja:久喜市]], {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|en}}[[ja:埼玉県]]) is regarded as the main shrine of Ōtori Shrines.<ref>In the {{ill|Kansai region|en}}[[ja:近畿地方]], {{ill|Ōtori Grand Shrine|en}}[[ja:大鳥大社]] (in {{ill|Sakai|en}}[[ja:堺市]], {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en}}[[ja:大阪府]]) is considered the main shrine (M. Okada, "Guide to Famous Shrines Nationwide," published by Tokyo Daijingu). The connection between Ōtori shrines across Kanto remains unclear.</ref> The enshrined deities are {{ill|Ame-no-Hohi|en}}[[ja:天穂日命]], {{ill|Takehi-Nateru|en}}[[ja:武夷鳥命|fr]], and {{ill|Ōkuninushi|en}}[[ja:大己貴命]]. Legend states that {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en}}[[ja:ヤマトタケル]] prayed for victory at the shrine during his eastern campaign. Over time, faith in "酉の日精進" (ritual abstinence on the Cock Day) spread, leading to the "大酉祭" (Great Cock Festival) held on the first Cock Day of December.
In the {{ill|Edo period|en}}[[ja:江戸時代]], the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|en}}[[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]] in {{ill|Hanahata Village|en}}[[ja:花畑 (足立区)]], {{ill|Musashi Province|en}}[[ja:武蔵国]], became famous and was referred to as "本酉" (Main Cock). The harvest festival held by local residents around this shrine is considered the origin of the Edo Cock Festival. Currently, the shrine enshrines Yamato Takeru, who is said to have celebrated his victory at this location after returning from his campaign. During the Edo period, the shrine’s deity was identified as {{ill|Shakyamuni|en}}[[ja:釈迦]], depicted riding on the back of a rooster. Historical records suggest that this festival dates back to the early 15th century during the {{ill|Ōei era|en}}[[ja:応永]]. Pilgrims offered roosters to pray for good fortune, later releasing them near {{ill|Sensō-ji|en}}[[ja:浅草寺]] in Asakusa after the festival ended.
By the late Edo period, the most prominent Cock Festival was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] and "酉の寺" {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|en}}[[ja:長国寺]] in Asakusa. During this time, the deity at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine was considered the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Myōken Bodhisattva|en}}[[ja:妙見菩薩]], riding on the back of a rooster. In Edo, the Cock Festivals were categorized as follows: the "上酉" (Upper Cock) or "本酉" (Main Cock) at Hanahata Ōtori Shrine, the "中酉" (Middle Cock) at {{ill|Shōsen-ji|en}}[[ja:勝専寺]] in Senju, and the "下酉" (Lower Cock) or "新酉" (New Cock) at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji. By the late Edo period, Cock Festivals were also held at shrines like those in Sugamo and Zōshigaya. In the Meiji era, the Cock Festival at Senju’s Shōsen-ji ceased, but many traditions from the Edo period persist to this day.
Asakusa's Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji Temple were located next to {{ill|Shin-Yoshiwara|en}}[[ja:新吉原]], a prominent red-light district. On festival days, the district would open its gates, adding to the popularity and renown of this Cock Festival. Today, it remains the largest Cock Festival in Japan, attracting approximately 70,000 to 80,000 visitors annually, with around 150 rake vendors and 750 food stalls. [[ja:酉の市]]
== Historical Development == During the late Edo period, the most famous Torinoichi was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] in {{ill|Asakusa|en}}[[ja:浅草]], along with the adjacent {{ill|Chōkoku-ji (Taitō Ward)|lt=Chōkokuji|en}}[[ja:長国寺 (台東区)]]. These events remain prominent, drawing crowds from all over Tokyo.
==Shrines and Temples Known for the Cock Festival== {{see also|{{ill|Ōtori Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲神社]]]] The Cock Festival, which rivals {{ill|Ebisu-kō|en}}[[ja:えびす講]] as a festival wishing for business prosperity, is primarily celebrated in the {{ill|Kantō region|en}}[[ja:関東地方]], where it originated. Unlike the Ebisu-kō, which is widely practiced not only in the {{ill|Keihanshin|en}}[[ja:京阪神]] area but also throughout both {{ill|Eastern Japan|en}}[[ja:東日本]] and {{ill|Western Japan|en}}[[ja:西日本]], the Cock Festival remains more localized around the Kantō region. Since the Meiji period, however, the festival has spread to some shrines and temples in {{ill|Hamamatsu|en}}[[ja:浜松市]], {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en}}[[ja:静岡県]], and {{ill|Toyohashi|en}}[[ja:豊橋市]], {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en}}[[ja:愛知県]]. In recent years, it has even been celebrated at shrines in the {{ill|Nakamura-ku|en}}[[ja:中村区]], {{ill|Nagoya|en}}[[ja:名古屋市]].<ref>At Susanoo Shrine in Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, the Cock Festival is held after enshrining deities from Ōtori Shrine as subsidiary deities. Other celebrations in the city, such as those at {{ill|Shichiji Temple|en}}[[ja:稲園山七寺]] (Ōsu Shichiji and Chōfukuji), are self-proclaimed Cock Festivals without clear historical connections to religious traditions.</ref>
The following are notable shrines and temples known for their Cock Festival celebrations. In addition to those listed, many other shrines in southern Kantō hold Cock Festivals (or rake markets): * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|en}}[[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]] (Adachi Ward, Tokyo) — The origin site of the Edo Cock Festival * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — One of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō, hosting Japan's largest Cock Festival, the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|en}}[[ja:長国寺 (台東区)]] (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — Known as the "酉の寺" (Cock Temple) and the birthplace of the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en}}[[ja:花園神社]] (Shinjuku Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the festival of a merged Ōtori Shrine and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|en}}[[ja:大國魂神社]] (Fuchū City, Tokyo) — The festival is hosted by its subsidiary shrine, Ōtori Shrine, and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Nerima Ōtori Shrine|en}}[[ja:練馬大鳥神社]] (Nerima Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the Cock Festival every November on Cock Days, attracting tens of thousands of visitors * {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲宮神社]] (Kuki, Saitama Prefecture) — Considered the origin of the Great Cock Festival and hosts a smaller rake market * {{ill|Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|en}}[[ja:熊野神社 (前橋市千代田町)]] (Maebashi, Gunma Prefecture) — Hosts the Maebashi Great Cock Festival, one of Maebashi's four major festivals * {{ill|Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|en}}[[ja:金刀比羅大鷲神社]] (Yokohama, Kanagawa Prefecture) — Its Cock Festival is recognized as an intangible cultural property of Yokohama
Although the {{ill|Ōtori taisha|en}}[[ja:大鳥神社]] in Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, is regarded as the head shrine of Ōtori faith, its "酉の日祭" (Cock Day Festival), held on the Cock Days in November,<ref>[http://www.ootoritaisha.jp/gyouji/ Ōtori Shrine official website]</ref> does not feature the rake markets or nighttime stalls typical of the Kantō region. [[ja:酉の市で知られる寺社]] ==Origin== The origin of the Cock Festival is explained differently by {{ill|Shinto|en}}[[ja:神道]] and {{ill|Buddhism|en}}[[ja:仏教]].
=== Shinto Explanation === According to Shinto traditions, the Cock Festival originated from markets held on the day of the Great Cock Festival (Ōtori Matsuri). The deities of Ōtori Shrine (or Washi Shrine) include {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en}}[[ja:ヤマトタケル]], who prayed for victory during his eastern campaign at {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en}}[[ja:鷲宮神社]]. He later celebrated his victory at the site of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|en}}[[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]] in Hanahata, which also commemorates the day of Yamato Takeru’s death. On November Cock Days (or December’s first Cock Day at Washinomiya Shrine), the Great Cock Festival is held. The shrine tradition of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] in Asakusa states that Yamato Takeru returned to give thanks on a November Cock Day and leaned his weapons against a pine tree in front of the shrine. This act led to the establishment of the Great Cock Festival and the use of decorative {{ill|rakes|en}}[[ja:熊手]] as auspicious items.
=== Buddhist Explanation === In Buddhist tradition, specifically at {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|en}}[[ja:長国寺 (台東区)]] in Asakusa, the Cock Festival originates from the market held during the unveiling (kaichō) of the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Washi Myōken Daibosatsu|en}}[[ja:鷲妙見大菩薩]]. On a November Cock Day in 1265 (Bun’ei 2), {{ill|Nichiren|en}}[[ja:日蓮]], the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|en}}[[ja:日蓮宗]], was staying at the Kobayakawa household in {{ill|Kazusa Province|en}}[[ja:上総国]] (present-day Mobara City, Chiba Prefecture). While praying for national peace, the morning star (Venus) shone brightly, and Washi Myōken Daibosatsu appeared riding on the back of an eagle. Since the establishment of Chōkoku-ji, the temple has held an annual market on November Cock Days, featuring the transfer of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu from Washiyama-dera. In 1771 (Meiwa 8), the statue of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu was enshrined permanently at Chōkoku-ji, where the annual Cock Festival continued.
=== Historical Practices === The festival is thought to have started as a harvest celebration by nearby farmers at the Hanahata Washi Daimyōjin shrine. Known also as the Rooster Daimyōjin, worshippers abstained from eating chicken meat, and even shrine families refrained from consuming eggs. Farmers offered live chickens as tributes, releasing them at the Asakusa Kannon Hall ({{ill|Sensō-ji|en}}[[ja:浅草寺]]) after the festival.
Because the shrine was conveniently located along the Ayase River, it became a hub for people and goods transported via waterways. As a result, the Cock Day markets gradually attracted visitors from all over Edo (Tokyo). Gambling flourished at these markets until bans during the An’ei era curtailed the festivities.
Eventually, the thriving Cock Festival shifted to the Asakusa Washi Daimyōjin, which became the most prominent venue. Its proximity to {{ill|Yoshiwara|en}}[[ja:吉原 (東京都)]], a famous red-light district, further contributed to its popularity. Over time, Cock Festivals spread across Edo and are now celebrated at many shrines and temples in the Kantō region.
Thus, the Cock Festival evolved from a rural agricultural market showcasing autumn harvests and farming tools into an urban celebration featuring auspicious decorative rakes symbolizing good fortune and prosperity. [[ja:酉の市の由来]]
==Customs== [[File:酉の市Torinoichi002.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The Cock Festival at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|en}}[[ja:大鷲神社 (足立区)]]. The shrine distributes auspicious {{ill|rakes|en}}[[ja:熊手]].]]
=== Rake Talismans and Decorative Rakes === On the days of the Cock Festival, stalls line up selling "decorative rakes" (engimono kumade), adorned with items such as okame masks and other symbols of good fortune. Shrines hosting the festival also distribute small bamboo {{ill|rakes|en}}[[ja:熊手]], adorned with rice ears and talismans, as "rake talismans" (kumade mamori). These rakes are colloquially called "kakkome," a pun meaning to "sweep in" or "gather in" blessings. Originally, rakes and {{ill|hoes|en}}[[ja:鍬]], along with other farming tools, were sold to local farmers around Washi Shrine on festival days. Over time, auspicious items such as okame masks began to be attached to the tools as complimentary gifts, evolving into today's decorative rakes.<ref>[http://www.torinoichi.jp/goriyaku/goriyaku_5.html Cock Festival Benefits]</ref>
The Cock Festival's auspicious items have included "tou no imo" (唐の芋, a type of yam) and "kogane mochi" (黄金餅, millet cakes), since the Edo period. The yam symbolized advancement and promotion due to its "head" shape, while its numerous offspring represented fertility. The millet cakes were believed to bring wealth. However, from the late Edo period, {{ill|kirizansho|en}}[[ja:切り山椒]], a type of sweet confection, replaced the millet cakes as a festival item. Eating kirizansho during this cold season is said to prevent colds.<ref>[http://www.otorisama.or.jp/mame.html About the Cock Festival]</ref>
The decorative rake is the festival's iconic auspicious item, symbolizing the talons of an {{ill|eagle|en}}[[ja:鷲]], which "grasp" its prey. The rake thus conveys the idea of gathering fortune or seizing prosperity. Decorative rakes are often bought through lively bargaining exchanges between rake sellers and buyers, where victorious negotiations are celebrated with exuberant {{ill|tejime|en}}[[ja:手締め]] hand clapping. The size of the decorative rakes tends to grow larger every year, reflecting sellers’ strategies and buyers’ desires for increasing fortune.
=== The Third Cock Day === The "Cock Day" (Tori no Hi) is determined using the {{ill|sexagenary cycle|en}}[[ja:干支]], occurring every twelve days.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/learning/elib/qa/qa_35.html |title=Is a Year with Three Cock Days More Prone to Fires? |access-date=2024-12-01 |publisher=Tokyo Fire Department]]</ref> Depending on the month’s alignment, November may have two or three Cock Days.<ref>For instance, if November 3 is the first Cock Day (Ichinotori), then November 15 will be the second (Ninotori), and November 27 the third (Sannotori). However, if November 8 is the first Cock Day, the second falls on November 20, and the next Cock Day occurs in December.</ref> The first Cock Day is called "Ichinotori," the second "Ninotori," and the third "Sannotori."
Years with three Cock Days are traditionally believed to have a higher incidence of fires, though there is no scientific basis for this claim.<ref name=":0" /> Consequently, in years with three Cock Days, greater care is taken with fire safety, especially in late December. Many rake merchants affix "Fire Safety" seals to their rakes during these years. Since three Cock Days occur approximately every other year, they are not particularly rare (see [[#List of Cock Days in November|List of Cock Days in November]]).
In Asakusa's {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|en}}[[ja:鷲神社 (台東区)]] and {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|en}}[[ja:長国寺 (台東区)]], a nearby {{ill|red-light district|en}}[[ja:吉原 (東京都)]] called [[:en:Yoshiwara|Yoshiwara]] contributed to a peculiar custom. It is said that wives would warn their husbands about the fire risk of the third Cock Day to prevent them from visiting Yoshiwara under the pretense of attending the festival.<ref>[http://ii-nippon.net/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AE%E7%A5%AD/891.html Japanese Festivals: Three Popular Theories]</ref>

[[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|{{ill|Torinoichi|ja|酉の市}} at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)}}}} '''Torinoichi''' (酉の市) is a festival held annually on the {{ill|Day of the Rooster|ja|酉}} in {{ill|November|ja|11月}}<ref>See {{anchor|List of "Days of the Rooster" in November|"Days of the Rooster" list}}.</ref>. It is also known as the '''Festival of the Rooster''' (酉の祭, Tori no Machi), '''Ōtori Festival''' (大酉祭, Ōtori Matsuri), or simply '''Otorisama''' (お酉様).
==Overview== [[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes at the {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|ja|花園神社}} in {{ill|Shinjuku|ja|新宿区}}, {{ill|Tokyo|ja|東京都}}, during the "酉の市" (Cock Festival).}} [[File:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|{{ill|Utagawa Hiroshige|ja|歌川広重}}'s ''{{ill|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|ja|名所江戸百景}},'' depicting the bustling visitors heading to {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)}} viewed from a brothel room in {{ill|Yoshiwara red-light district|ja|吉原遊廓}}.<ref>The image echoes this scene with a hairpin in the bottom left shaped like a {{ill|good-luck rake|ja|熊手}}, decorated with suggestive elements such as {{ill|Okame|ja|おかめ}} and matsutake mushrooms.</ref>}} [[File:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes during the "酉の市" at the subsidiary shrine {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Fuchū)|ja|大國魂神社}}.}}
The "酉の市" (Cock Festival) is an annual event associated with shrines and temples linked to roosters or birds, such as {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社}}, "酉の寺," and {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社}}. Predominantly celebrated in the Kanto region, the festival is famous for its vibrant atmosphere, with many stalls selling {{ill|good-luck rakes|ja|熊手}} amidst vigorous hand-clapping rituals. It is a well-known year-end tradition.
At {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社}}, which enshrines {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル}}, the deity is venerated as a patron of lasting military fortune, prosperity, and success in business. In the Kanto region, {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社}} (in {{ill|Kuki|ja|久喜市}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県}}) is regarded as the main shrine of Ōtori Shrines.<ref>In the {{ill|Kansai region|ja|近畿地方}}, {{ill|Ōtori Grand Shrine|ja|大鳥大社}} (in {{ill|Sakai|ja|堺市}}, {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}) is considered the main shrine (M. Okada, "Guide to Famous Shrines Nationwide," published by Tokyo Daijingu). The connection between Ōtori shrines across Kanto remains unclear.</ref> The enshrined deities are {{ill|Ame-no-Hohi|ja|天穂日命}}, {{ill|Takehi-Nateru|ja|武夷鳥命|fr}}, and {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命}}. Legend states that {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル}} prayed for victory at the shrine during his eastern campaign. Over time, faith in "酉の日精進" (ritual abstinence on the Cock Day) spread, leading to the "大酉祭" (Great Cock Festival) held on the first Cock Day of December.
In the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代}}, the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)}} in {{ill|Hanahata Village|ja|花畑 (足立区)}}, {{ill|Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国}}, became famous and was referred to as "本酉" (Main Cock). The harvest festival held by local residents around this shrine is considered the origin of the Edo Cock Festival. Currently, the shrine enshrines Yamato Takeru, who is said to have celebrated his victory at this location after returning from his campaign. During the Edo period, the shrine’s deity was identified as {{ill|Shakyamuni|ja|釈迦}}, depicted riding on the back of a rooster. Historical records suggest that this festival dates back to the early 15th century during the {{ill|Ōei era|ja|応永}}. Pilgrims offered roosters to pray for good fortune, later releasing them near {{ill|Sensō-ji|ja|浅草寺}} in Asakusa after the festival ended.
By the late Edo period, the most prominent Cock Festival was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)}} and "酉の寺" {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺}} in Asakusa. During this time, the deity at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine was considered the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Myōken Bodhisattva|ja|妙見菩薩}}, riding on the back of a rooster. In Edo, the Cock Festivals were categorized as follows: the "上酉" (Upper Cock) or "本酉" (Main Cock) at Hanahata Ōtori Shrine, the "中酉" (Middle Cock) at {{ill|Shōsen-ji|ja|勝専寺}} in Senju, and the "下酉" (Lower Cock) or "新酉" (New Cock) at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji. By the late Edo period, Cock Festivals were also held at shrines like those in Sugamo and Zōshigaya. In the Meiji era, the Cock Festival at Senju’s Shōsen-ji ceased, but many traditions from the Edo period persist to this day.
Asakusa's Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji Temple were located next to {{ill|Shin-Yoshiwara|ja|新吉原}}, a prominent red-light district. On festival days, the district would open its gates, adding to the popularity and renown of this Cock Festival. Today, it remains the largest Cock Festival in Japan, attracting approximately 70,000 to 80,000 visitors annually, with around 150 rake vendors and 750 food stalls. [[ja:酉の市}}
== Historical Development == During the late Edo period, the most famous Torinoichi was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)}} in {{ill|Asakusa|ja|浅草}}, along with the adjacent {{ill|Chōkoku-ji (Taitō Ward)|lt=Chōkokuji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)}}. These events remain prominent, drawing crowds from all over Tokyo.
==Shrines and Temples Known for the Cock Festival== {{see also|{{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社}}}} The Cock Festival, which rivals {{ill|Ebisu-kō|ja|えびす講}} as a festival wishing for business prosperity, is primarily celebrated in the {{ill|Kantō region|ja|関東地方}}, where it originated. Unlike the Ebisu-kō, which is widely practiced not only in the {{ill|Keihanshin|ja|京阪神}} area but also throughout both {{ill|Eastern Japan|ja|東日本}} and {{ill|Western Japan|ja|西日本}}, the Cock Festival remains more localized around the Kantō region. Since the Meiji period, however, the festival has spread to some shrines and temples in {{ill|Hamamatsu|ja|浜松市}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|ja|静岡県}}, and {{ill|Toyohashi|ja|豊橋市}}, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|ja|愛知県}}. In recent years, it has even been celebrated at shrines in the {{ill|Nakamura-ku|ja|中村区}}, {{ill|Nagoya|ja|名古屋市}}.<ref>At Susanoo Shrine in Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, the Cock Festival is held after enshrining deities from Ōtori Shrine as subsidiary deities. Other celebrations in the city, such as those at {{ill|Shichiji Temple|ja|稲園山七寺}} (Ōsu Shichiji and Chōfukuji), are self-proclaimed Cock Festivals without clear historical connections to religious traditions.</ref>
The following are notable shrines and temples known for their Cock Festival celebrations. In addition to those listed, many other shrines in southern Kantō hold Cock Festivals (or rake markets): * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)}} (Adachi Ward, Tokyo) — The origin site of the Edo Cock Festival * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — One of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō, hosting Japan's largest Cock Festival, the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — Known as the "酉の寺" (Cock Temple) and the birthplace of the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|ja|花園神社}} (Shinjuku Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the festival of a merged Ōtori Shrine and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|ja|大國魂神社}} (Fuchū City, Tokyo) — The festival is hosted by its subsidiary shrine, Ōtori Shrine, and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Nerima Ōtori Shrine|ja|練馬大鳥神社}} (Nerima Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the Cock Festival every November on Cock Days, attracting tens of thousands of visitors * {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社}} (Kuki, Saitama Prefecture) — Considered the origin of the Great Cock Festival and hosts a smaller rake market * {{ill|Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|ja|熊野神社 (前橋市千代田町)}} (Maebashi, Gunma Prefecture) — Hosts the Maebashi Great Cock Festival, one of Maebashi's four major festivals * {{ill|Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|ja|金刀比羅大鷲神社}} (Yokohama, Kanagawa Prefecture) — Its Cock Festival is recognized as an intangible cultural property of Yokohama
Although the {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社}} in Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, is regarded as the head shrine of Ōtori faith, its "酉の日祭" (Cock Day Festival), held on the Cock Days in November,<ref>[http://www.ootoritaisha.jp/gyouji/ Ōtori Shrine official website]</ref> does not feature the rake markets or nighttime stalls typical of the Kantō region. [[ja:酉の市で知られる寺社}} ==Origin== The origin of the Cock Festival is explained differently by {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}} and {{ill|Buddhism|ja|仏教}}.
=== Shinto Explanation === According to Shinto traditions, the Cock Festival originated from markets held on the day of the Great Cock Festival (Ōtori Matsuri). The deities of Ōtori Shrine (or Washi Shrine) include {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル}}, who prayed for victory during his eastern campaign at {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社}}. He later celebrated his victory at the site of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)}} in Hanahata, which also commemorates the day of Yamato Takeru’s death. On November Cock Days (or December’s first Cock Day at Washinomiya Shrine), the Great Cock Festival is held. The shrine tradition of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)}} in Asakusa states that Yamato Takeru returned to give thanks on a November Cock Day and leaned his weapons against a pine tree in front of the shrine. This act led to the establishment of the Great Cock Festival and the use of decorative {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手}} as auspicious items.
=== Buddhist Explanation === In Buddhist tradition, specifically at {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)}} in Asakusa, the Cock Festival originates from the market held during the unveiling (kaichō) of the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Washi Myōken Daibosatsu|ja|鷲妙見大菩薩}}. On a November Cock Day in 1265 (Bun’ei 2), {{ill|Nichiren|ja|日蓮}}, the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|ja|日蓮宗}}, was staying at the Kobayakawa household in {{ill|Kazusa Province|ja|上総国}} (present-day Mobara City, Chiba Prefecture). While praying for national peace, the morning star (Venus) shone brightly, and Washi Myōken Daibosatsu appeared riding on the back of an eagle. Since the establishment of Chōkoku-ji, the temple has held an annual market on November Cock Days, featuring the transfer of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu from Washiyama-dera. In 1771 (Meiwa 8), the statue of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu was enshrined permanently at Chōkoku-ji, where the annual Cock Festival continued.
=== Historical Practices === The festival is thought to have started as a harvest celebration by nearby farmers at the Hanahata Washi Daimyōjin shrine. Known also as the Rooster Daimyōjin, worshippers abstained from eating chicken meat, and even shrine families refrained from consuming eggs. Farmers offered live chickens as tributes, releasing them at the Asakusa Kannon Hall ({{ill|Sensō-ji|ja|浅草寺}}) after the festival.
Because the shrine was conveniently located along the Ayase River, it became a hub for people and goods transported via waterways. As a result, the Cock Day markets gradually attracted visitors from all over Edo (Tokyo). Gambling flourished at these markets until bans during the An’ei era curtailed the festivities.
Eventually, the thriving Cock Festival shifted to the Asakusa Washi Daimyōjin, which became the most prominent venue. Its proximity to {{ill|Yoshiwara|ja|吉原 (東京都)}}, a famous red-light district, further contributed to its popularity. Over time, Cock Festivals spread across Edo and are now celebrated at many shrines and temples in the Kantō region.
Thus, the Cock Festival evolved from a rural agricultural market showcasing autumn harvests and farming tools into an urban celebration featuring auspicious decorative rakes symbolizing good fortune and prosperity. [[ja:酉の市の由来}}
