[[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|[[鷲神社 (台東区)]]の酉の市]] '''酉の市'''（とりのいち）は、例年[[11月]]の[[酉|酉の日]]<ref>[[#11月の「酉の日」一覧|11月の「酉の日」一覧]]を参照。</ref>に行われる[[祭]]。'''酉の祭'''（とりのまち）、'''大酉祭'''（おおとりまつり）、'''お酉様'''（おとりさま）ともいう。
==概説== [[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|[[花園神社]]（[[東京都]][[新宿区]]）の「酉の市」で、縁起熊手を売る露店]] [[ファイル:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|[[歌川広重]]『[[名所江戸百景]]』より「浅草田圃酉の町」。[[吉原遊廓|吉原妓楼]]の一室から、[[鷲神社 (台東区)|鷲神社]]へ参る人の賑いを遠くに望む<ref>なお、遠景に呼応するように左下にも[[熊手]]をかたどった簪（かんざし）を描き込んでいるが、こちらは[[おかめ]]と松茸を配した、やや艶っぽい暗示のものとなっている。</ref>。]] [[ファイル:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|[[大國魂神社]]の末社・大鷲神社の「酉の市」で、縁起熊手を売る露店。]]
酉の市は、[[鷲神社]]、酉の寺、大鳥神社など鷲や鳥にちなむ寺社の[[年中行事]]として知られ、関東地方を中心とする祭りである。多くの露店で、威勢よく[[手締め]]して「[[熊手#縁起物としての熊手|縁起熊手]]」を売る祭の賑わいは、[[年末]]の[[風物詩]]である。
鷲神社は、[[ヤマトタケル|日本武尊]]（やまとたけるのみこと）を祀り、武運長久、開運、商売繁盛の神として信仰される。関東地方では[[鷲宮神社]]（[[埼玉県]][[久喜市]]）が鷲神社の本社とされる<ref>[[近畿地方|関西地方]]では[[大鳥大社]]（[[大阪府]][[堺市]]）が本社とされる（岡田米夫「全国著名神社案内記」東京大神宮刊）。関東各地にある鷲神社との関係は明らかでない。</ref>。同社の祭神は、[[天穂日命]]、[[武夷鳥命]]、[[大己貴命]]である。日本武尊が[[ヤマトタケル#東征|東征]]の際、同社で戦勝を祈願したとされる。古くからこの神社を中心に「酉の日精進」の信仰が広まり、12月の初酉の日には大酉祭が行われる。
[[江戸時代]]には、[[武蔵国]][[南足立郡]]花又村（現・東京都[[足立区]][[花畑 (足立区)|花畑]]）にある[[大鷲神社 (足立区)|大鷲神社]]（鷲大明神）が栄え、「本酉」と言われた。この花又鷲大明神を産土神とする近在住民の収穫祭が、江戸酉の市の発祥とされる。現在の同社の祭神は日本武尊で、東征からの帰還の際、同地で戦勝を祝したとされる。江戸時代には、花又の鷲大明神（[[神仏習合#本地垂迹説|本地]]）は鷲の背に乗った[[釈迦]]とされた。この神社の酉の市は、15世紀初めの[[応永]]年間に始まるとされ、参詣人は、[[ニワトリ|鶏]]を献納して開運を祈り、祭が終了した後浅草観音堂前（[[浅草寺]]）に献納した鶏を放った。
江戸時代後期から、最も著名な酉の市は、[[浅草]]の[[鷲神社 (台東区)|鷲神社]]（おおとりじんじゃ）と酉の寺 長國寺（とりのてら ちょうこくじ）境内で行われた酉の市である。江戸時代には浅草の鷲大明神（[[神仏習合#本地垂迹説|本地]]）は鷲の背に乗る妙見菩薩とされた。「現在の足立区花畑の大鷲神社を「上酉、本酉」、千住にある[[勝専寺]]を「中酉」、浅草の鷲神社と酉の寺 長國寺を「下酉、新酉」と称しており、江戸時代に盛大な酉の市はこの3カ所であった。幕末には巣鴨、雑司ヶ谷などの大鳥神社でも酉の市が開催されるようになる。明治時代になると千住・勝専寺の酉の市は閉鎖されたが、江戸時代から続く酉の市はいくつかあり現在も賑わっている。
浅草の鷲神社と酉の寺 長國寺の東隣には新吉原という遊郭が存在し、酉の市御例祭の日には遊郭内が開放されたといわれ、地の利も加わり最も有名な酉の市として現在に至る。規模（熊手店約150店舗・露天約750店）賑わい（毎年70万人～80万人の人出）とも日本一の酉の市である。
==酉の市で知られる寺社== {{see also|鷲神社}} 酉の市は、商売繁盛を願う祭りとしては[[えびす講]]と双璧をなすものであるが、えびす講が[[京阪神]]を中心に[[西日本]]のみならず[[東日本]]でも広く行われているものであるのに対し、発祥の地である[[関東地方]]周辺に限局する傾向が強く見られる。なお、明治以降[[静岡県]][[浜松市]]、[[愛知県]][[豊橋市]]の一部の寺社でも開催されるようになり、近年では[[名古屋市]][[中村区]]の神社でも行われるようになっている<ref>名古屋市中村区の素盞男神社では摂社に鷲神社から祭神を勧請の上で酉の市が行われている。なお同市の稲園山七寺（大須七寺、長福寺）などで行われているものは、自称酉の市と称するが神仏に関する由緒が判然としない。</ref>。 酉の市を開催することで知られる著名な寺社には以下のものがある。下記以外にも関東地方南部で酉の市（熊手市）を行う寺社は複数ある。 * [[大鷲神社 (足立区)|大鷲神社]]（東京都[[足立区]]） ※江戸酉の市の発祥の神社 * [[鷲神社 (台東区)|鷲神社]]（東京都[[台東区]]） ※関東三大酉の市のひとつで日本最大の酉の市、浅草酉の市が行われる * [[長国寺 (台東区)|酉の寺・長國寺]]（東京都台東区）※浅草酉の市の発祥の寺 * [[花園神社]]（東京都[[新宿区]]） ※合祀された大鳥神社の祭りであり、関東三大酉の市のひとつ * [[大國魂神社]]（東京都[[府中市 (東京都)|府中市]]） ※境内末社の大鷲神社の祭りであり、関東三大酉の市のひとつ * [[練馬大鳥神社]]（東京都練馬区） ※毎年11月の酉の日に酉の市をとり行い、数万人の人が訪れ賑わいを見せる。 * [[鷲宮神社]]（[[埼玉県]][[久喜市]]） ※大酉祭の元祖とされ、小規模ながら熊手市も行われる * [[熊野神社 (前橋市千代田町)|熊野神社]]（[[群馬県]][[前橋市]]） ※前橋の四大まつりのひとつ、[[前橋大酉祭]]が行われる * [[金刀比羅大鷲神社]]（[[神奈川県]][[横浜市]]） ※酉の市は横浜市の無形民俗文化財
<!--著名な寺社--> なお大鳥信仰の総本社とされる[[大鳥大社]]（大阪府堺市西区）では、11月酉の日に「酉の日祭」<ref>[http://www.ootoritaisha.jp/gyouji/ 大鳥神社ホームページ]</ref>の祭礼はあるものの、関東地方のような熊手市や夜の屋台は無い。
==由来== 酉の市の由来は、[[神道]]と[[仏教]]の双方から、それぞれ異なる解説がされる。
神道の解説では、大酉祭の日に立った市を、酉の市の起源とする。大鳥神社（鷲神社）の祭神である日本武尊が、東征の戦勝祈願を鷲宮神社で行い、祝勝を花畑の大鷲神社の地で行った。これにちなみ、日本武尊が亡くなった日とされる11月の酉の日（鷲宮神社では12月の初酉の日）には大酉祭が行われる。また、浅草・鷲神社の社伝では、日本武尊が鷲神社に戦勝のお礼参りをしたのが11月の酉の日であり、その際、社前の松に武具の[[熊手]]を立て掛けたことから、大酉祭を行い、熊手を縁起物とするとしている。
仏教（浅草酉の寺・[[長国寺 (台東区)|長國寺]]）の解説では、鷲妙見大菩薩の開帳日に立った市を酉の市の起源とする。[[1265年]]（[[文永]]2年）11月の酉の日、[[日蓮宗]]の宗祖・[[日蓮]]が、[[上総国]]鷲巣（現・[[千葉県]][[茂原市]]）の小早川家（現・大本山鷲山寺）に滞在の折、国家平穏を祈ったところ、明星（[[金星]]）が明るく輝きだし、鷲妙見大菩薩が鷲の背に乗り現れ出た。これにちなみ、浅草の長國寺では、創建以来、11月の酉の日に鷲山寺から鷲妙見大菩薩の出開帳が行われた。その後1771年（明和8年）長國寺に鷲妙見大菩薩（鷲大明神）が勧請され、11月の酉の日に開帳されるようになった。
実際の祭りは、花又の鷲大明神の近在農民による収穫祭が発端といわれる。鷲大明神は鶏大明神とも呼ばれ当時氏子は鶏肉を食べる事を忌み、社家は鶏卵さえ食べない。近郷農民は生きた鶏を奉納し祭が終わると浅草寺観音堂前に放ったのである。このように鶏を神とも祀った社は、綾瀬川に面しているため水運による人、物の集合に好適であった。そのため酉の日に立つ市には江戸市中からの参詣者も次第に多くなり、そこでは社前で辻賭博が盛大に開帳されたが安永年間に出された禁止令により賑わいは衰微する。
かわって、酉の市の盛況ぶりは浅草の鷲大明神へと移り、最も賑わう酉の市として現在に至るのである。また浅草鷲大明神の東隣に新吉原が控えていたことも浅草酉の市が盛況を誇る大きな要因であった。時代が下るにつれ江戸の各地で酉の市が開かれるようになり、今では関東の多くの寺社で開催されるようになった。
このように酉の市とは、秋の収穫物や実用の農具が並んだ近郊農村の農業市が江戸市中へと移行するに従い、招福の吉兆を満載した飾り[[熊手]]などを市の縁起物とする都市型の祭へと変遷してきたのである。
==習俗== [[File:酉の市Torinoichi002.jpg|thumb|right|300px|大鷲神社の酉の市。神社が[[熊手]]を頒布している。]] ===熊手守りと縁起熊手=== 「酉の市」の立つ日には、おかめや招福の縁起物を飾った「縁起熊手」を売る露店が立ち並ぶ。また、市を開催する寺社からは小さな竹[[熊手]]に稲穂や札をつけた「熊手守り」が授与され、福を「掃き込む、かきこむ」との洒落にことよせ「かっこめ」と呼ばれている。元々は鷲神社周辺の農民のために縁日の境内で熊手や[[鍬]]などの[[農具]]を販売していたのが、次第に[[おかめ]]などの縁起物がオマケとして農具につけられるようになり、それが今日の装飾熊手の由来となっている<ref>[http://www.torinoichi.jp/goriyaku/goriyaku_5.html 酉の市] ご利益</ref>。
酉の市の縁起物は、江戸時代より熊手の他に「頭の芋（とうのいも）」（唐の芋）や粟でつくった「黄金餅（こがねもち）」があった。頭の芋は頭（かしら）になって出世する、芋は子芋を数多く付ける事から子宝に恵まれるとされ、黄金餅は金持ちになれるといわれた。しかし幕末頃から売られるようになった「[[切り山椒]]」が黄金餅に変わって市の縁起物となり今日にいたっている。本格的な寒さを迎えるこの時期、これを食べれば風邪を引かないといわれる<ref>[http://www.otorisama.or.jp/mame.html お酉様]</ref>。
縁起物の代表である熊手は、[[鷲]]が獲物をわしづかみすることになぞらえ、その爪を模したともいわれ、福徳をかき集める、鷲づかむという意味が込められている。熊手は熊手商と買った（勝った）、まけた（負けた）と気っ風の良いやり取りを楽しんで買うものとされ、商談が成立すると威勢よく[[手締め]]が打たれる（商品額をまけさせて、その差し引いた分を店側に「ご祝儀」として渡すことを「[[粋]]な買い方」とする人もおり、手締めはこの「ご祝儀」を店側が受け取った場合に行われる場合が多い。つまり、この方法でいくと結局は定額を支払っているわけだが、ご祝儀については明確に決まっているわけではなく、差し引き分以上の場合もあれば、小銭程度であったりと買い手側の意思に依存している）。熊手は大小様々なものが売られており、主に売り手の思惑により年々大きくしてゆくものともされている。
=== 三の酉 === 「酉の日」は、毎日に[[干支|十干十二支]]を当てて定める日付け法で「酉」に当たる日のこと。酉の日は12日おきに巡ってくる<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/learning/elib/qa/qa_35.html |title=三の酉の年は火災が多い？ |access-date=2024-12-01 |publisher=東京消防庁}}</ref>。ひと月は30日なので、日の巡り合わせにより、11月の酉の日は2回の年と3回の年がある<ref>例えば、11月3日が酉の日（一の酉）の年の場合、12日後の15日（二の酉）、さらに12日後の27日（三の酉）が酉の日に当たり、11月中に3回、酉の日が生じる。しかし、11月8日が酉の日（一の酉）の年の場合、次の20日（二の酉）との2回、11月中に酉の日が生じ、その次の酉の日は12月2日となる。結局、11月1日から6日までに一の酉がある年は三の酉まで生じ、7日から12日までに一の酉がある年は二の酉までとなる。</ref>。初酉を「一の酉」、次を「二の酉」、3番目を「三の酉」と言う。「三の酉」まである年は[[火事]]が多いと言われるが、その確証はない<ref name=":0" />。そのため、三の酉がある年には平年にもまして、歳末にかけて、社会一般で火の用心が心がけられ、熊手[[商人|商]]の多くは縁起[[熊手]]に「火の用心」のシールを貼って売りだす。なお、三の酉は、およそ一年おきにあるため、さほど珍しいわけではない（''「[[#11月の「酉の日」一覧|11月の「酉の日」一覧]]」を参照''）。
また、浅草の[[鷲神社 (台東区)|鷲神社]]・酉の寺 長國寺では、[[吉原 (東京都)|吉原]]が近かった為、'''酉の市'''にかこつけて旦那衆が家を空け吉原に遊びに行くのを防ぐために、家の女房が三の酉は火事が多いと言ったとの説もある<ref>[http://ii-nippon.net/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AE%E7%A5%AD/891.html 日本の祭り] 3つの俗説</ref>。

[[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|{{ill|Torinoichi|ja|酉の市|1=Tori-no-Ichi|qq=draft|qq=draft}} at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] '''Torinoichi''' (酉の市) is a festival held annually on the {{ill|Rooster (zodiac)|ja|酉|1=Rooster (zodiac)|2=ja|3=酉|4=fr|5=Coq (astrologie chinoise)|6=nl|7=Haan (astrologie)|lt=Rooster (酉)|Rooster (zodiac)=Rooster (zodiac)|lt=Day of the Rooster|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|November|ja|11月|qq=draft|qq=draft}}<ref>See {{anchor|List of "Days of the Rooster" in November|"Days of the Rooster" list}}.</ref>. It is also known as the '''Festival of the Rooster''' (酉の祭, Tori no Machi), '''Ōtori Festival''' (大酉祭, Ōtori Matsuri), or simply '''Otorisama''' (お酉様).
==Overview== [[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes at the {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|ja|花園神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|Shinjuku|ja|新宿区|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Tokyo|ja|東京都|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, during the "酉の市" (Cock Festival).}]] [[File:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|{{ill|Utagawa Hiroshige|ja|歌川広重|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s ''{{ill|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|ja|名所江戸百景|qq=draft|qq=draft}},'' depicting the bustling visitors heading to {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} viewed from a brothel room in {{ill|Yoshiwara red-light district|ja|吉原遊廓|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>The image echoes this scene with a hairpin in the bottom left shaped like a {{ill|good-luck rake|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, decorated with suggestive elements such as {{ill|Okame|ja|おかめ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and matsutake mushrooms.</ref>]] [[File:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes during the "酉の市" at the subsidiary shrine {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Fuchū)|ja|大國魂神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.]]
The "酉の市" (Cock Festival) is an annual event associated with shrines and temples linked to roosters or birds, such as {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, "酉の寺," and {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Predominantly celebrated in the Kanto region, the festival is famous for its vibrant atmosphere, with many stalls selling {{ill|rake|ja|熊手|lt=good-luck rakes|qq=draft|qq=draft}} amidst vigorous hand-clapping rituals. It is a well-known year-end tradition.
At {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which enshrines {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the deity is venerated as a patron of lasting military fortune, prosperity, and success in business. In the Kanto region, {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社|1=Washinomiya Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (in {{ill|Kuki|ja|久喜市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) is regarded as the main shrine of Ōtori Shrines.<ref>In the {{ill|Kansai region|ja|近畿地方|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Ōtori Grand Shrine|ja|大鳥大社|1=Ōtori taisha|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (in {{ill|Sakai|ja|堺市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) is considered the main shrine (M. Okada, "Guide to Famous Shrines Nationwide," published by Tokyo Daijingu). The connection between Ōtori shrines across Kanto remains unclear.</ref> The enshrined deities are {{ill|Ame-no-Hohi|ja|天穂日命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Takehi-Nateru|ja|武夷鳥命|fr|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Legend states that {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft}} prayed for victory at the shrine during his eastern campaign. Over time, faith in "酉の日精進" (ritual abstinence on the Cock Day) spread, leading to the "大酉祭" (Great Cock Festival) held on the first Cock Day of December.
In the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|Hanahata Village|ja|花畑 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, became famous and was referred to as "本酉" (Main Cock). The harvest festival held by local residents around this shrine is considered the origin of the Edo Cock Festival. Currently, the shrine enshrines Yamato Takeru, who is said to have celebrated his victory at this location after returning from his campaign. During the Edo period, the shrine’s deity was identified as {{ill|Shakyamuni|ja|釈迦|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, depicted riding on the back of a rooster. Historical records suggest that this festival dates back to the early 15th century during the {{ill|Ōei era|ja|応永|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Pilgrims offered roosters to pray for good fortune, later releasing them near {{ill|Sensō-ji|ja|浅草寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa after the festival ended.
By the late Edo period, the most prominent Cock Festival was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and "酉の寺" {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa. During this time, the deity at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine was considered the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Myōken Bodhisattva|ja|妙見菩薩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, riding on the back of a rooster. In Edo, the Cock Festivals were categorized as follows: the "上酉" (Upper Cock) or "本酉" (Main Cock) at Hanahata Ōtori Shrine, the "中酉" (Middle Cock) at {{ill|Shōsen-ji|ja|勝専寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Senju, and the "下酉" (Lower Cock) or "新酉" (New Cock) at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji. By the late Edo period, Cock Festivals were also held at shrines like those in Sugamo and Zōshigaya. In the Meiji era, the Cock Festival at Senju’s Shōsen-ji ceased, but many traditions from the Edo period persist to this day.
Asakusa's Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji Temple were located next to {{ill|Shin-Yoshiwara|ja|新吉原|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a prominent red-light district. On festival days, the district would open its gates, adding to the popularity and renown of this Cock Festival. Today, it remains the largest Cock Festival in Japan, attracting approximately 70,000 to 80,000 visitors annually, with around 150 rake vendors and 750 food stalls.
== Historical Development == During the late Edo period, the most famous Torinoichi was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|Asakusa|ja|浅草|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, along with the adjacent {{ill|Chōkoku-ji (Taitō Ward)|lt=Chōkokuji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. These events remain prominent, drawing crowds from all over Tokyo.
==Shrines and Temples Known for the Cock Festival== {{see also|{{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}}} The Cock Festival, which rivals {{ill|Ebisu-kō|ja|えびす講|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as a festival wishing for business prosperity, is primarily celebrated in the {{ill|Kantō region|ja|関東地方|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, where it originated. Unlike the Ebisu-kō, which is widely practiced not only in the {{ill|Keihanshin|ja|京阪神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} area but also throughout both {{ill|Eastern Japan|ja|東日本|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Western Japan|ja|西日本|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the Cock Festival remains more localized around the Kantō region. Since the Meiji period, however, the festival has spread to some shrines and temples in {{ill|Hamamatsu|ja|浜松市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|ja|静岡県|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Toyohashi|ja|豊橋市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|ja|愛知県|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In recent years, it has even been celebrated at shrines in the {{ill|Nakamura-ku|ja|中村区|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Nagoya|ja|名古屋市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>At Susanoo Shrine in Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, the Cock Festival is held after enshrining deities from Ōtori Shrine as subsidiary deities. Other celebrations in the city, such as those at {{ill|Shichiji Temple|ja|稲園山七寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Ōsu Shichiji and Chōfukuji), are self-proclaimed Cock Festivals without clear historical connections to religious traditions.</ref>
The following are notable shrines and temples known for their Cock Festival celebrations. In addition to those listed, many other shrines in southern Kantō hold Cock Festivals (or rake markets): * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Adachi Ward, Tokyo) — The origin site of the Edo Cock Festival * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — One of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō, hosting Japan's largest Cock Festival, the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — Known as the "酉の寺" (Cock Temple) and the birthplace of the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|ja|花園神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Shinjuku Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the festival of a merged Ōtori Shrine and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|ja|大國魂神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Fuchū City, Tokyo) — The festival is hosted by its subsidiary shrine, Ōtori Shrine, and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Nerima Ōtori Shrine|ja|練馬大鳥神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Nerima Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the Cock Festival every November on Cock Days, attracting tens of thousands of visitors * {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社|1=Washinomiya Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Kuki, Saitama Prefecture) — Considered the origin of the Great Cock Festival and hosts a smaller rake market * {{ill|Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|ja|熊野神社 (前橋市千代田町)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Maebashi, Gunma Prefecture) — Hosts the Maebashi Great Cock Festival, one of Maebashi's four major festivals * {{ill|Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|ja|金刀比羅大鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Yokohama, Kanagawa Prefecture) — Its Cock Festival is recognized as an intangible cultural property of Yokohama
Although the {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, is regarded as the head shrine of Ōtori faith, its "酉の日祭" (Cock Day Festival), held on the Cock Days in November,<ref>[http://www.ootoritaisha.jp/gyouji/ Ōtori Shrine official website]</ref> does not feature the rake markets or nighttime stalls typical of the Kantō region.
==Origin== The origin of the Cock Festival is explained differently by {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Buddhism|ja|仏教|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
=== Shinto Explanation === According to Shinto traditions, the Cock Festival originated from markets held on the day of the Great Cock Festival (Ōtori Matsuri). The deities of Ōtori Shrine (or Washi Shrine) include {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, who prayed for victory during his eastern campaign at {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社|1=Washinomiya Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. He later celebrated his victory at the site of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Hanahata, which also commemorates the day of Yamato Takeru’s death. On November Cock Days (or December’s first Cock Day at Washinomiya Shrine), the Great Cock Festival is held. The shrine tradition of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa states that Yamato Takeru returned to give thanks on a November Cock Day and leaned his weapons against a pine tree in front of the shrine. This act led to the establishment of the Great Cock Festival and the use of decorative {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as auspicious items.
=== Buddhist Explanation === In Buddhist tradition, specifically at {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa, the Cock Festival originates from the market held during the unveiling (kaichō) of the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Washi Myōken Daibosatsu|ja|鷲妙見大菩薩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. On a November Cock Day in 1265 (Bun’ei 2), {{ill|Nichiren|ja|Nichiren|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|ja|Nichiren宗|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, was staying at the Kobayakawa household in {{ill|Kazusa Province|ja|上総国|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (present-day Mobara City, Chiba Prefecture). While praying for national peace, the morning star (Venus) shone brightly, and Washi Myōken Daibosatsu appeared riding on the back of an eagle. Since the establishment of Chōkoku-ji, the temple has held an annual market on November Cock Days, featuring the transfer of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu from Washiyama-dera. In 1771 (Meiwa 8), the statue of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu was enshrined permanently at Chōkoku-ji, where the annual Cock Festival continued.
=== Historical Practices === The festival is thought to have started as a harvest celebration by nearby farmers at the Hanahata Washi Daimyōjin shrine. Known also as the Rooster Daimyōjin, worshippers abstained from eating chicken meat, and even shrine families refrained from consuming eggs. Farmers offered live chickens as tributes, releasing them at the Asakusa Kannon Hall ({{ill|Sensō-ji|ja|浅草寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) after the festival.
Because the shrine was conveniently located along the Ayase River, it became a hub for people and goods transported via waterways. As a result, the Cock Day markets gradually attracted visitors from all over Edo (Tokyo). Gambling flourished at these markets until bans during the An’ei era curtailed the festivities.
Eventually, the thriving Cock Festival shifted to the Asakusa Washi Daimyōjin, which became the most prominent venue. Its proximity to {{ill|Yoshiwara|ja|吉原 (東京都)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a famous red-light district, further contributed to its popularity. Over time, Cock Festivals spread across Edo and are now celebrated at many shrines and temples in the Kantō region.
Thus, the Cock Festival evolved from a rural agricultural market showcasing autumn harvests and farming tools into an urban celebration featuring auspicious decorative rakes symbolizing good fortune and prosperity.
==Customs== [[File:酉の市Torinoichi002.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The Cock Festival at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. The shrine distributes auspicious {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.]]
=== Rake Talismans and Decorative Rakes === On the days of the Cock Festival, stalls line up selling "decorative rakes" (engimono kumade), adorned with items such as okame masks and other symbols of good fortune. Shrines hosting the festival also distribute small bamboo {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, adorned with rice ears and talismans, as "rake talismans" (kumade mamori). These rakes are colloquially called "kakkome," a pun meaning to "sweep in" or "gather in" blessings. Originally, rakes and {{ill|hoes|ja|鍬|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, along with other farming tools, were sold to local farmers around Washi Shrine on festival days. Over time, auspicious items such as okame masks began to be attached to the tools as complimentary gifts, evolving into today's decorative rakes.<ref>[http://www.torinoichi.jp/goriyaku/goriyaku_5.html Cock Festival Benefits]</ref>
The Cock Festival's auspicious items have included "tou no imo" (唐の芋, a type of yam) and "kogane mochi" (黄金餅, millet cakes), since the Edo period. The yam symbolized advancement and promotion due to its "head" shape, while its numerous offspring represented fertility. The millet cakes were believed to bring wealth. However, from the late Edo period, {{ill|kirizansho|ja|切り山椒|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a type of sweet confection, replaced the millet cakes as a festival item. Eating kirizansho during this cold season is said to prevent colds.<ref>[http://www.otorisama.or.jp/mame.html About the Cock Festival]</ref>
The decorative rake is the festival's iconic auspicious item, symbolizing the talons of an {{ill|eagle|ja|鷲|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which "grasp" its prey. The rake thus conveys the idea of gathering fortune or seizing prosperity. Decorative rakes are often bought through lively bargaining exchanges between rake sellers and buyers, where victorious negotiations are celebrated with exuberant {{ill|tejime|ja|手締め|qq=draft|qq=draft}} hand clapping. The size of the decorative rakes tends to grow larger every year, reflecting sellers’ strategies and buyers’ desires for increasing fortune.
=== The Third Cock Day === The "Cock Day" (Tori no Hi) is determined using the {{ill|sexagenary cycle|ja|干支|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, occurring every twelve days.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/learning/elib/qa/qa_35.html |title=Is a Year with Three Cock Days More Prone to Fires? |access-date=2024-12-01 |publisher=Tokyo Fire Department}}</ref> Depending on the month’s alignment, November may have two or three Cock Days.<ref>For instance, if November 3 is the first Cock Day (Ichinotori), then November 15 will be the second (Ninotori), and November 27 the third (Sannotori). However, if November 8 is the first Cock Day, the second falls on November 20, and the next Cock Day occurs in December.</ref> The first Cock Day is called "Ichinotori," the second "Ninotori," and the third "Sannotori."
Years with three Cock Days are traditionally believed to have a higher incidence of fires, though there is no scientific basis for this claim.<ref name=":0" /> Consequently, in years with three Cock Days, greater care is taken with fire safety, especially in late December. Many rake merchants affix "Fire Safety" seals to their rakes during these years. Since three Cock Days occur approximately every other year, they are not particularly rare (see [[#List of Cock Days in November|List of Cock Days in November]]).
In Asakusa's {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a nearby {{ill|red-light district|ja|吉原 (東京都)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} called [[:en:Yoshiwara|Yoshiwara]] contributed to a peculiar custom. It is said that wives would warn their husbands about the fire risk of the third Cock Day to prevent them from visiting Yoshiwara under the pretense of attending the festival.<ref>[http://ii-nippon.net/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AE%E7%A5%AD/891.html Japanese Festivals: Three Popular Theories]</ref>

<!--Tori-no-Ichi--> <!--Tori-no-Ichi--> {{translated page|ja|酉の市|version=103103842|comment=Imported full ja history}}

[[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|{{ill|Torinoichi|ja|酉の市|1=Tori-no-Ichi|qq=draft|qq=draft}} at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] '''Torinoichi''' (酉の市) is a festival held annually on the {{ill|Rooster (zodiac)|ja|酉|1=Rooster (zodiac)|2=ja|3=酉|4=fr|5=Coq (astrologie chinoise)|6=nl|7=Haan (astrologie)|lt=Rooster (酉)|Rooster (zodiac)=Rooster (zodiac)|lt=Day of the Rooster|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|November|ja|11月|qq=draft|qq=draft}}<ref>See {{anchor|List of "Days of the Rooster" in November|"Days of the Rooster" list}}.</ref>. It is also known as the '''Festival of the Rooster''' (酉の祭, Tori no Machi), '''Ōtori Festival''' (大酉祭, Ōtori Matsuri), or simply '''Otorisama''' (お酉様).
==Overview== [[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes at the {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|ja|花園神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|Shinjuku|ja|新宿区|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Tokyo|ja|東京都|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, during the "酉の市" (Cock Festival).}]] [[File:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|{{ill|Utagawa Hiroshige|ja|歌川広重|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s ''{{ill|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|ja|名所江戸百景|qq=draft|qq=draft}},'' depicting the bustling visitors heading to {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} viewed from a brothel room in {{ill|Yoshiwara red-light district|ja|吉原遊廓|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>The image echoes this scene with a hairpin in the bottom left shaped like a {{ill|good-luck rake|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, decorated with suggestive elements such as {{ill|Okame|ja|おかめ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and matsutake mushrooms.</ref>]] [[File:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes during the "酉の市" at the subsidiary shrine {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Fuchū)|ja|大國魂神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.]]
The "酉の市" (Cock Festival) is an annual event associated with shrines and temples linked to roosters or birds, such as {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, "酉の寺," and {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Predominantly celebrated in the Kanto region, the festival is famous for its vibrant atmosphere, with many stalls selling {{ill|rake|ja|熊手|lt=good-luck rakes|qq=draft|qq=draft}} amidst vigorous hand-clapping rituals. It is a well-known year-end tradition.
At {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which enshrines {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the deity is venerated as a patron of lasting military fortune, prosperity, and success in business. In the Kanto region, {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社|1=Washinomiya Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (in {{ill|Kuki|ja|久喜市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) is regarded as the main shrine of Ōtori Shrines.<ref>In the {{ill|Kansai region|ja|近畿地方|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Ōtori Grand Shrine|ja|大鳥大社|1=Ōtori taisha|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (in {{ill|Sakai|ja|堺市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) is considered the main shrine (M. Okada, "Guide to Famous Shrines Nationwide," published by Tokyo Daijingu). The connection between Ōtori shrines across Kanto remains unclear.</ref> The enshrined deities are {{ill|Ame-no-Hohi|ja|天穂日命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Takehi-Nateru|ja|武夷鳥命|fr|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Legend states that {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft}} prayed for victory at the shrine during his eastern campaign. Over time, faith in "酉の日精進" (ritual abstinence on the Cock Day) spread, leading to the "大酉祭" (Great Cock Festival) held on the first Cock Day of December.
In the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|Hanahata Village|ja|花畑 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, became famous and was referred to as "本酉" (Main Cock). The harvest festival held by local residents around this shrine is considered the origin of the Edo Cock Festival. Currently, the shrine enshrines Yamato Takeru, who is said to have celebrated his victory at this location after returning from his campaign. During the Edo period, the shrine’s deity was identified as {{ill|Shakyamuni|ja|釈迦|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, depicted riding on the back of a rooster. Historical records suggest that this festival dates back to the early 15th century during the {{ill|Ōei era|ja|応永|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Pilgrims offered roosters to pray for good fortune, later releasing them near {{ill|Sensō-ji|ja|浅草寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa after the festival ended.
By the late Edo period, the most prominent Cock Festival was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and "酉の寺" {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa. During this time, the deity at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine was considered the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Myōken Bodhisattva|ja|妙見菩薩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, riding on the back of a rooster. In Edo, the Cock Festivals were categorized as follows: the "上酉" (Upper Cock) or "本酉" (Main Cock) at Hanahata Ōtori Shrine, the "中酉" (Middle Cock) at {{ill|Shōsen-ji|ja|勝専寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Senju, and the "下酉" (Lower Cock) or "新酉" (New Cock) at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji. By the late Edo period, Cock Festivals were also held at shrines like those in Sugamo and Zōshigaya. In the Meiji era, the Cock Festival at Senju’s Shōsen-ji ceased, but many traditions from the Edo period persist to this day.
Asakusa's Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji Temple were located next to {{ill|Shin-Yoshiwara|ja|新吉原|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a prominent red-light district. On festival days, the district would open its gates, adding to the popularity and renown of this Cock Festival. Today, it remains the largest Cock Festival in Japan, attracting approximately 70,000 to 80,000 visitors annually, with around 150 rake vendors and 750 food stalls.
== Historical Development == During the late Edo period, the most famous Torinoichi was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|Asakusa|ja|浅草|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, along with the adjacent {{ill|Chōkoku-ji (Taitō Ward)|lt=Chōkokuji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. These events remain prominent, drawing crowds from all over Tokyo.
==Shrines and Temples Known for the Cock Festival== {{see also|{{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}}} The Cock Festival, which rivals {{ill|Ebisu-kō|ja|えびす講|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as a festival wishing for business prosperity, is primarily celebrated in the {{ill|Kantō region|ja|関東地方|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, where it originated. Unlike the Ebisu-kō, which is widely practiced not only in the {{ill|Keihanshin|ja|京阪神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} area but also throughout both {{ill|Eastern Japan|ja|東日本|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Western Japan|ja|西日本|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the Cock Festival remains more localized around the Kantō region. Since the Meiji period, however, the festival has spread to some shrines and temples in {{ill|Hamamatsu|ja|浜松市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|ja|静岡県|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Toyohashi|ja|豊橋市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|ja|愛知県|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In recent years, it has even been celebrated at shrines in the {{ill|Nakamura-ku|ja|中村区|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Nagoya|ja|名古屋市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>At Susanoo Shrine in Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, the Cock Festival is held after enshrining deities from Ōtori Shrine as subsidiary deities. Other celebrations in the city, such as those at {{ill|Shichiji Temple|ja|稲園山七寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Ōsu Shichiji and Chōfukuji), are self-proclaimed Cock Festivals without clear historical connections to religious traditions.</ref>
The following are notable shrines and temples known for their Cock Festival celebrations. In addition to those listed, many other shrines in southern Kantō hold Cock Festivals (or rake markets): * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Adachi Ward, Tokyo) — The origin site of the Edo Cock Festival * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — One of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō, hosting Japan's largest Cock Festival, the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — Known as the "酉の寺" (Cock Temple) and the birthplace of the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|ja|花園神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Shinjuku Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the festival of a merged Ōtori Shrine and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|ja|大國魂神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Fuchū City, Tokyo) — The festival is hosted by its subsidiary shrine, Ōtori Shrine, and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Nerima Ōtori Shrine|ja|練馬大鳥神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Nerima Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the Cock Festival every November on Cock Days, attracting tens of thousands of visitors * {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社|1=Washinomiya Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Kuki, Saitama Prefecture) — Considered the origin of the Great Cock Festival and hosts a smaller rake market * {{ill|Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|ja|熊野神社 (前橋市千代田町)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Maebashi, Gunma Prefecture) — Hosts the Maebashi Great Cock Festival, one of Maebashi's four major festivals * {{ill|Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|ja|金刀比羅大鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Yokohama, Kanagawa Prefecture) — Its Cock Festival is recognized as an intangible cultural property of Yokohama
Although the {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, is regarded as the head shrine of Ōtori faith, its "酉の日祭" (Cock Day Festival), held on the Cock Days in November,<ref>[http://www.ootoritaisha.jp/gyouji/ Ōtori Shrine official website]</ref> does not feature the rake markets or nighttime stalls typical of the Kantō region.
==Origin== The origin of the Cock Festival is explained differently by {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Buddhism|ja|仏教|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
=== Shinto Explanation === According to Shinto traditions, the Cock Festival originated from markets held on the day of the Great Cock Festival (Ōtori Matsuri). The deities of Ōtori Shrine (or Washi Shrine) include {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, who prayed for victory during his eastern campaign at {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社|1=Washinomiya Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. He later celebrated his victory at the site of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Hanahata, which also commemorates the day of Yamato Takeru’s death. On November Cock Days (or December’s first Cock Day at Washinomiya Shrine), the Great Cock Festival is held. The shrine tradition of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa states that Yamato Takeru returned to give thanks on a November Cock Day and leaned his weapons against a pine tree in front of the shrine. This act led to the establishment of the Great Cock Festival and the use of decorative {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as auspicious items.
=== Buddhist Explanation === In Buddhist tradition, specifically at {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa, the Cock Festival originates from the market held during the unveiling (kaichō) of the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Washi Myōken Daibosatsu|ja|鷲妙見大菩薩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. On a November Cock Day in 1265 (Bun’ei 2), {{ill|Nichiren|ja|Nichiren|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|ja|Nichiren宗|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, was staying at the Kobayakawa household in {{ill|Kazusa Province|ja|上総国|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (present-day Mobara City, Chiba Prefecture). While praying for national peace, the morning star (Venus) shone brightly, and Washi Myōken Daibosatsu appeared riding on the back of an eagle. Since the establishment of Chōkoku-ji, the temple has held an annual market on November Cock Days, featuring the transfer of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu from Washiyama-dera. In 1771 (Meiwa 8), the statue of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu was enshrined permanently at Chōkoku-ji, where the annual Cock Festival continued.
=== Historical Practices === The festival is thought to have started as a harvest celebration by nearby farmers at the Hanahata Washi Daimyōjin shrine. Known also as the Rooster Daimyōjin, worshippers abstained from eating chicken meat, and even shrine families refrained from consuming eggs. Farmers offered live chickens as tributes, releasing them at the Asakusa Kannon Hall ({{ill|Sensō-ji|ja|浅草寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) after the festival.
Because the shrine was conveniently located along the Ayase River, it became a hub for people and goods transported via waterways. As a result, the Cock Day markets gradually attracted visitors from all over Edo (Tokyo). Gambling flourished at these markets until bans during the An’ei era curtailed the festivities.
Eventually, the thriving Cock Festival shifted to the Asakusa Washi Daimyōjin, which became the most prominent venue. Its proximity to {{ill|Yoshiwara|ja|吉原 (東京都)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a famous red-light district, further contributed to its popularity. Over time, Cock Festivals spread across Edo and are now celebrated at many shrines and temples in the Kantō region.
Thus, the Cock Festival evolved from a rural agricultural market showcasing autumn harvests and farming tools into an urban celebration featuring auspicious decorative rakes symbolizing good fortune and prosperity.
==Customs== [[File:酉の市Torinoichi002.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The Cock Festival at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. The shrine distributes auspicious {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.]]
=== Rake Talismans and Decorative Rakes === On the days of the Cock Festival, stalls line up selling "decorative rakes" (engimono kumade), adorned with items such as okame masks and other symbols of good fortune. Shrines hosting the festival also distribute small bamboo {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, adorned with rice ears and talismans, as "rake talismans" (kumade mamori). These rakes are colloquially called "kakkome," a pun meaning to "sweep in" or "gather in" blessings. Originally, rakes and {{ill|hoes|ja|鍬|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, along with other farming tools, were sold to local farmers around Washi Shrine on festival days. Over time, auspicious items such as okame masks began to be attached to the tools as complimentary gifts, evolving into today's decorative rakes.<ref>[http://www.torinoichi.jp/goriyaku/goriyaku_5.html Cock Festival Benefits]</ref>
The Cock Festival's auspicious items have included "tou no imo" (唐の芋, a type of yam) and "kogane mochi" (黄金餅, millet cakes), since the Edo period. The yam symbolized advancement and promotion due to its "head" shape, while its numerous offspring represented fertility. The millet cakes were believed to bring wealth. However, from the late Edo period, {{ill|kirizansho|ja|切り山椒|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a type of sweet confection, replaced the millet cakes as a festival item. Eating kirizansho during this cold season is said to prevent colds.<ref>[http://www.otorisama.or.jp/mame.html About the Cock Festival]</ref>
The decorative rake is the festival's iconic auspicious item, symbolizing the talons of an {{ill|eagle|ja|鷲|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which "grasp" its prey. The rake thus conveys the idea of gathering fortune or seizing prosperity. Decorative rakes are often bought through lively bargaining exchanges between rake sellers and buyers, where victorious negotiations are celebrated with exuberant {{ill|tejime|ja|手締め|qq=draft|qq=draft}} hand clapping. The size of the decorative rakes tends to grow larger every year, reflecting sellers’ strategies and buyers’ desires for increasing fortune.
=== The Third Cock Day === The "Cock Day" (Tori no Hi) is determined using the {{ill|sexagenary cycle|ja|干支|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, occurring every twelve days.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/learning/elib/qa/qa_35.html |title=Is a Year with Three Cock Days More Prone to Fires? |access-date=2024-12-01 |publisher=Tokyo Fire Department}}</ref> Depending on the month’s alignment, November may have two or three Cock Days.<ref>For instance, if November 3 is the first Cock Day (Ichinotori), then November 15 will be the second (Ninotori), and November 27 the third (Sannotori). However, if November 8 is the first Cock Day, the second falls on November 20, and the next Cock Day occurs in December.</ref> The first Cock Day is called "Ichinotori," the second "Ninotori," and the third "Sannotori."
Years with three Cock Days are traditionally believed to have a higher incidence of fires, though there is no scientific basis for this claim.<ref name=":0" /> Consequently, in years with three Cock Days, greater care is taken with fire safety, especially in late December. Many rake merchants affix "Fire Safety" seals to their rakes during these years. Since three Cock Days occur approximately every other year, they are not particularly rare (see [[#List of Cock Days in November|List of Cock Days in November]]).
In Asakusa's {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a nearby {{ill|red-light district|ja|吉原 (東京都)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} called [[:en:Yoshiwara|Yoshiwara]] contributed to a peculiar custom. It is said that wives would warn their husbands about the fire risk of the third Cock Day to prevent them from visiting Yoshiwara under the pretense of attending the festival.<ref>[http://ii-nippon.net/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AE%E7%A5%AD/891.html Japanese Festivals: Three Popular Theories]</ref>

revision.text:
[[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|{{ill|Torinoichi|ja|酉の市|1=Tori-no-Ichi|qq=draft|qq=draft}} at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] '''Torinoichi''' (酉の市) is a festival held annually on the {{ill|Rooster (zodiac)|ja|酉|1=Rooster (zodiac)|2=ja|3=酉|4=fr|5=Coq (astrologie chinoise)|6=nl|7=Haan (astrologie)|lt=Rooster (酉)|Rooster (zodiac)=Rooster (zodiac)|lt=Day of the Rooster|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|November|ja|11月|qq=draft|qq=draft}}<ref>See {{anchor|List of "Days of the Rooster" in November|"Days of the Rooster" list}}.</ref>. It is also known as the '''Festival of the Rooster''' (酉の祭, Tori no Machi), '''Ōtori Festival''' (大酉祭, Ōtori Matsuri), or simply '''Otorisama''' (お酉様).
==Overview== [[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes at the {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|ja|花園神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|Shinjuku|ja|新宿区|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Tokyo|ja|東京都|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, during the "酉の市" (Cock Festival).}]] [[File:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|{{ill|Utagawa Hiroshige|ja|歌川広重|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s ''{{ill|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|ja|名所江戸百景|qq=draft|qq=draft}},'' depicting the bustling visitors heading to {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} viewed from a brothel room in {{ill|Yoshiwara red-light district|ja|吉原遊廓|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>The image echoes this scene with a hairpin in the bottom left shaped like a {{ill|good-luck rake|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, decorated with suggestive elements such as {{ill|Okame|ja|おかめ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and matsutake mushrooms.</ref>]] [[File:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes during the "酉の市" at the subsidiary shrine {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Fuchū)|ja|大國魂神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.]]
The "酉の市" (Cock Festival) is an annual event associated with shrines and temples linked to roosters or birds, such as {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, "酉の寺," and {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Predominantly celebrated in the Kanto region, the festival is famous for its vibrant atmosphere, with many stalls selling {{ill|rake|ja|熊手|lt=good-luck rakes|qq=draft|qq=draft}} amidst vigorous hand-clapping rituals. It is a well-known year-end tradition.
At {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which enshrines {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the deity is venerated as a patron of lasting military fortune, prosperity, and success in business. In the Kanto region, {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社|1=Washinomiya Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (in {{ill|Kuki|ja|久喜市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) is regarded as the main shrine of Ōtori Shrines.<ref>In the {{ill|Kansai region|ja|近畿地方|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Ōtori Grand Shrine|ja|大鳥大社|1=Ōtori taisha|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (in {{ill|Sakai|ja|堺市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) is considered the main shrine (M. Okada, "Guide to Famous Shrines Nationwide," published by Tokyo Daijingu). The connection between Ōtori shrines across Kanto remains unclear.</ref> The enshrined deities are {{ill|Ame-no-Hohi|ja|天穂日命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Takehi-Nateru|ja|武夷鳥命|fr|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Legend states that {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft}} prayed for victory at the shrine during his eastern campaign. Over time, faith in "酉の日精進" (ritual abstinence on the Cock Day) spread, leading to the "大酉祭" (Great Cock Festival) held on the first Cock Day of December.
In the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|Hanahata Village|ja|花畑 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, became famous and was referred to as "本酉" (Main Cock). The harvest festival held by local residents around this shrine is considered the origin of the Edo Cock Festival. Currently, the shrine enshrines Yamato Takeru, who is said to have celebrated his victory at this location after returning from his campaign. During the Edo period, the shrine’s deity was identified as {{ill|Shakyamuni|ja|釈迦|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, depicted riding on the back of a rooster. Historical records suggest that this festival dates back to the early 15th century during the {{ill|Ōei era|ja|応永|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Pilgrims offered roosters to pray for good fortune, later releasing them near {{ill|Sensō-ji|ja|浅草寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa after the festival ended.
By the late Edo period, the most prominent Cock Festival was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and "酉の寺" {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa. During this time, the deity at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine was considered the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Myōken Bodhisattva|ja|妙見菩薩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, riding on the back of a rooster. In Edo, the Cock Festivals were categorized as follows: the "上酉" (Upper Cock) or "本酉" (Main Cock) at Hanahata Ōtori Shrine, the "中酉" (Middle Cock) at {{ill|Shōsen-ji|ja|勝専寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Senju, and the "下酉" (Lower Cock) or "新酉" (New Cock) at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji. By the late Edo period, Cock Festivals were also held at shrines like those in Sugamo and Zōshigaya. In the Meiji era, the Cock Festival at Senju’s Shōsen-ji ceased, but many traditions from the Edo period persist to this day.
Asakusa's Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji Temple were located next to {{ill|Shin-Yoshiwara|ja|新吉原|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a prominent red-light district. On festival days, the district would open its gates, adding to the popularity and renown of this Cock Festival. Today, it remains the largest Cock Festival in Japan, attracting approximately 70,000 to 80,000 visitors annually, with around 150 rake vendors and 750 food stalls.
== Historical Development == During the late Edo period, the most famous Torinoichi was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|Asakusa|ja|浅草|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, along with the adjacent {{ill|Chōkoku-ji (Taitō Ward)|lt=Chōkokuji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. These events remain prominent, drawing crowds from all over Tokyo.
==Shrines and Temples Known for the Cock Festival== {{see also|{{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}}} The Cock Festival, which rivals {{ill|Ebisu-kō|ja|えびす講|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as a festival wishing for business prosperity, is primarily celebrated in the {{ill|Kantō region|ja|関東地方|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, where it originated. Unlike the Ebisu-kō, which is widely practiced not only in the {{ill|Keihanshin|ja|京阪神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} area but also throughout both {{ill|Eastern Japan|ja|東日本|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Western Japan|ja|西日本|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the Cock Festival remains more localized around the Kantō region. Since the Meiji period, however, the festival has spread to some shrines and temples in {{ill|Hamamatsu|ja|浜松市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|ja|静岡県|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Toyohashi|ja|豊橋市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|ja|愛知県|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In recent years, it has even been celebrated at shrines in the {{ill|Nakamura-ku|ja|中村区|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Nagoya|ja|名古屋市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>At Susanoo Shrine in Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, the Cock Festival is held after enshrining deities from Ōtori Shrine as subsidiary deities. Other celebrations in the city, such as those at {{ill|Shichiji Temple|ja|稲園山七寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Ōsu Shichiji and Chōfukuji), are self-proclaimed Cock Festivals without clear historical connections to religious traditions.</ref>
The following are notable shrines and temples known for their Cock Festival celebrations. In addition to those listed, many other shrines in southern Kantō hold Cock Festivals (or rake markets): * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Adachi Ward, Tokyo) — The origin site of the Edo Cock Festival * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — One of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō, hosting Japan's largest Cock Festival, the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — Known as the "酉の寺" (Cock Temple) and the birthplace of the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|ja|花園神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Shinjuku Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the festival of a merged Ōtori Shrine and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|ja|大國魂神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Fuchū City, Tokyo) — The festival is hosted by its subsidiary shrine, Ōtori Shrine, and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Nerima Ōtori Shrine|ja|練馬大鳥神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Nerima Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the Cock Festival every November on Cock Days, attracting tens of thousands of visitors * {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社|1=Washinomiya Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Kuki, Saitama Prefecture) — Considered the origin of the Great Cock Festival and hosts a smaller rake market * {{ill|Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|ja|熊野神社 (前橋市千代田町)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Maebashi, Gunma Prefecture) — Hosts the Maebashi Great Cock Festival, one of Maebashi's four major festivals * {{ill|Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|ja|金刀比羅・大鷲神社|1=Konpira and Ōtori Shrine|2=ja|3=金刀比羅・大鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Yokohama, Kanagawa Prefecture) — Its Cock Festival is recognized as an intangible cultural property of Yokohama
Although the {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, is regarded as the head shrine of Ōtori faith, its "酉の日祭" (Cock Day Festival), held on the Cock Days in November,<ref>[http://www.ootoritaisha.jp/gyouji/ Ōtori Shrine official website]</ref> does not feature the rake markets or nighttime stalls typical of the Kantō region.
==Origin== The origin of the Cock Festival is explained differently by {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Buddhism|ja|仏教|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
=== Shinto Explanation === According to Shinto traditions, the Cock Festival originated from markets held on the day of the Great Cock Festival (Ōtori Matsuri). The deities of Ōtori Shrine (or Washi Shrine) include {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, who prayed for victory during his eastern campaign at {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社|1=Washinomiya Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. He later celebrated his victory at the site of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Hanahata, which also commemorates the day of Yamato Takeru’s death. On November Cock Days (or December’s first Cock Day at Washinomiya Shrine), the Great Cock Festival is held. The shrine tradition of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa states that Yamato Takeru returned to give thanks on a November Cock Day and leaned his weapons against a pine tree in front of the shrine. This act led to the establishment of the Great Cock Festival and the use of decorative {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as auspicious items.
=== Buddhist Explanation === In Buddhist tradition, specifically at {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa, the Cock Festival originates from the market held during the unveiling (kaichō) of the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Washi Myōken Daibosatsu|ja|鷲妙見大菩薩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. On a November Cock Day in 1265 (Bun’ei 2), {{ill|Nichiren|ja|Nichiren|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|ja|Nichiren宗|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, was staying at the Kobayakawa household in {{ill|Kazusa Province|ja|上総国|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (present-day Mobara City, Chiba Prefecture). While praying for national peace, the morning star (Venus) shone brightly, and Washi Myōken Daibosatsu appeared riding on the back of an eagle. Since the establishment of Chōkoku-ji, the temple has held an annual market on November Cock Days, featuring the transfer of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu from Washiyama-dera. In 1771 (Meiwa 8), the statue of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu was enshrined permanently at Chōkoku-ji, where the annual Cock Festival continued.
=== Historical Practices === The festival is thought to have started as a harvest celebration by nearby farmers at the Hanahata Washi Daimyōjin shrine. Known also as the Rooster Daimyōjin, worshippers abstained from eating chicken meat, and even shrine families refrained from consuming eggs. Farmers offered live chickens as tributes, releasing them at the Asakusa Kannon Hall ({{ill|Sensō-ji|ja|浅草寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) after the festival.
Because the shrine was conveniently located along the Ayase River, it became a hub for people and goods transported via waterways. As a result, the Cock Day markets gradually attracted visitors from all over Edo (Tokyo). Gambling flourished at these markets until bans during the An’ei era curtailed the festivities.
Eventually, the thriving Cock Festival shifted to the Asakusa Washi Daimyōjin, which became the most prominent venue. Its proximity to {{ill|Yoshiwara|ja|吉原 (東京都)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a famous red-light district, further contributed to its popularity. Over time, Cock Festivals spread across Edo and are now celebrated at many shrines and temples in the Kantō region.
Thus, the Cock Festival evolved from a rural agricultural market showcasing autumn harvests and farming tools into an urban celebration featuring auspicious decorative rakes symbolizing good fortune and prosperity.
==Customs== [[File:酉の市Torinoichi002.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The Cock Festival at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. The shrine distributes auspicious {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.]]
=== Rake Talismans and Decorative Rakes === On the days of the Cock Festival, stalls line up selling "decorative rakes" (engimono kumade), adorned with items such as okame masks and other symbols of good fortune. Shrines hosting the festival also distribute small bamboo {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, adorned with rice ears and talismans, as "rake talismans" (kumade mamori). These rakes are colloquially called "kakkome," a pun meaning to "sweep in" or "gather in" blessings. Originally, rakes and {{ill|hoes|ja|鍬|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, along with other farming tools, were sold to local farmers around Washi Shrine on festival days. Over time, auspicious items such as okame masks began to be attached to the tools as complimentary gifts, evolving into today's decorative rakes.<ref>[http://www.torinoichi.jp/goriyaku/goriyaku_5.html Cock Festival Benefits]</ref>
The Cock Festival's auspicious items have included "tou no imo" (唐の芋, a type of yam) and "kogane mochi" (黄金餅, millet cakes), since the Edo period. The yam symbolized advancement and promotion due to its "head" shape, while its numerous offspring represented fertility. The millet cakes were believed to bring wealth. However, from the late Edo period, {{ill|kirizansho|ja|切り山椒|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a type of sweet confection, replaced the millet cakes as a festival item. Eating kirizansho during this cold season is said to prevent colds.<ref>[http://www.otorisama.or.jp/mame.html About the Cock Festival]</ref>
The decorative rake is the festival's iconic auspicious item, symbolizing the talons of an {{ill|eagle|ja|鷲|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which "grasp" its prey. The rake thus conveys the idea of gathering fortune or seizing prosperity. Decorative rakes are often bought through lively bargaining exchanges between rake sellers and buyers, where victorious negotiations are celebrated with exuberant {{ill|tejime|ja|手締め|qq=draft|qq=draft}} hand clapping. The size of the decorative rakes tends to grow larger every year, reflecting sellers’ strategies and buyers’ desires for increasing fortune.
=== The Third Cock Day === The "Cock Day" (Tori no Hi) is determined using the {{ill|sexagenary cycle|ja|干支|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, occurring every twelve days.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/learning/elib/qa/qa_35.html |title=Is a Year with Three Cock Days More Prone to Fires? |access-date=2024-12-01 |publisher=Tokyo Fire Department}}</ref> Depending on the month’s alignment, November may have two or three Cock Days.<ref>For instance, if November 3 is the first Cock Day (Ichinotori), then November 15 will be the second (Ninotori), and November 27 the third (Sannotori). However, if November 8 is the first Cock Day, the second falls on November 20, and the next Cock Day occurs in December.</ref> The first Cock Day is called "Ichinotori," the second "Ninotori," and the third "Sannotori."
Years with three Cock Days are traditionally believed to have a higher incidence of fires, though there is no scientific basis for this claim.<ref name=":0" /> Consequently, in years with three Cock Days, greater care is taken with fire safety, especially in late December. Many rake merchants affix "Fire Safety" seals to their rakes during these years. Since three Cock Days occur approximately every other year, they are not particularly rare (see [[#List of Cock Days in November|List of Cock Days in November]]).
In Asakusa's {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a nearby {{ill|red-light district|ja|吉原 (東京都)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} called [[:en:Yoshiwara|Yoshiwara]] contributed to a peculiar custom. It is said that wives would warn their husbands about the fire risk of the third Cock Day to prevent them from visiting Yoshiwara under the pretense of attending the festival.<ref>[http://ii-nippon.net/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AE%E7%A5%AD/891.html Japanese Festivals: Three Popular Theories]</ref>

[[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|{{ill|Torinoichi|ja|酉の市|1=Tori-no-Ichi|qq=draft|qq=draft}} at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] '''Torinoichi''' (酉の市) is a festival held annually on the {{ill|Rooster (zodiac)|ja|酉|1=Rooster (zodiac)|2=ja|3=酉|4=fr|5=Coq (astrologie chinoise)|6=nl|7=Haan (astrologie)|lt=Rooster (酉)|Rooster (zodiac)=Rooster (zodiac)|lt=Day of the Rooster|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|November|ja|11月|qq=draft|qq=draft}}<ref>See {{anchor|List of "Days of the Rooster" in November|"Days of the Rooster" list}}.</ref>. It is also known as the '''Festival of the Rooster''' (酉の祭, Tori no Machi), '''Ōtori Festival''' (大酉祭, Ōtori Matsuri), or simply '''Otorisama''' (お酉様).
==Overview== [[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes at the {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|ja|花園神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|Shinjuku|ja|新宿区|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Tokyo|ja|東京都|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, during the "酉の市" (Cock Festival).}]] [[File:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|{{ill|Utagawa Hiroshige|ja|歌川広重|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s ''{{ill|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|ja|名所江戸百景|qq=draft|qq=draft}},'' depicting the bustling visitors heading to {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} viewed from a brothel room in {{ill|Yoshiwara red-light district|ja|吉原遊廓|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>The image echoes this scene with a hairpin in the bottom left shaped like a {{ill|good-luck rake|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, decorated with suggestive elements such as {{ill|Okame|ja|おかめ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and matsutake mushrooms.</ref>]] [[File:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes during the "酉の市" at the subsidiary shrine {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Fuchū)|ja|大國魂神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.]]
The "酉の市" (Cock Festival) is an annual event associated with shrines and temples linked to roosters or birds, such as {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, "酉の寺," and {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Predominantly celebrated in the Kanto region, the festival is famous for its vibrant atmosphere, with many stalls selling {{ill|rake|ja|熊手|lt=good-luck rakes|qq=draft|qq=draft}} amidst vigorous hand-clapping rituals. It is a well-known year-end tradition.
At {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which enshrines {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the deity is venerated as a patron of lasting military fortune, prosperity, and success in business. In the Kanto region, {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社|1=Washinomiya Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (in {{ill|Kuki|ja|久喜市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|ja|埼玉県|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) is regarded as the main shrine of Ōtori Shrines.<ref>In the {{ill|Kansai region|ja|近畿地方|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Ōtori Grand Shrine|ja|大鳥大社|1=Ōtori taisha|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (in {{ill|Sakai|ja|堺市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) is considered the main shrine (M. Okada, "Guide to Famous Shrines Nationwide," published by Tokyo Daijingu). The connection between Ōtori shrines across Kanto remains unclear.</ref> The enshrined deities are {{ill|Ame-no-Hohi|ja|天穂日命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Takehi-Nateru|ja|武夷鳥命|fr|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Legend states that {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft}} prayed for victory at the shrine during his eastern campaign. Over time, faith in "酉の日精進" (ritual abstinence on the Cock Day) spread, leading to the "大酉祭" (Great Cock Festival) held on the first Cock Day of December.
In the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|Hanahata Village|ja|花畑 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Musashi Province|ja|武蔵国|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, became famous and was referred to as "本酉" (Main Cock). The harvest festival held by local residents around this shrine is considered the origin of the Edo Cock Festival. Currently, the shrine enshrines Yamato Takeru, who is said to have celebrated his victory at this location after returning from his campaign. During the Edo period, the shrine’s deity was identified as {{ill|Shakyamuni|ja|釈迦|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, depicted riding on the back of a rooster. Historical records suggest that this festival dates back to the early 15th century during the {{ill|Ōei era|ja|応永|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Pilgrims offered roosters to pray for good fortune, later releasing them near {{ill|Sensō-ji|ja|浅草寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa after the festival ended.
By the late Edo period, the most prominent Cock Festival was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and "酉の寺" {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa. During this time, the deity at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine was considered the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Myōken Bodhisattva|ja|妙見菩薩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, riding on the back of a rooster. In Edo, the Cock Festivals were categorized as follows: the "上酉" (Upper Cock) or "本酉" (Main Cock) at Hanahata Ōtori Shrine, the "中酉" (Middle Cock) at {{ill|Shōsen-ji|ja|勝専寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Senju, and the "下酉" (Lower Cock) or "新酉" (New Cock) at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji. By the late Edo period, Cock Festivals were also held at shrines like those in Sugamo and Zōshigaya. In the Meiji era, the Cock Festival at Senju’s Shōsen-ji ceased, but many traditions from the Edo period persist to this day.
Asakusa's Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji Temple were located next to {{ill|Shin-Yoshiwara|ja|新吉原|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a prominent red-light district. On festival days, the district would open its gates, adding to the popularity and renown of this Cock Festival. Today, it remains the largest Cock Festival in Japan, attracting approximately 70,000 to 80,000 visitors annually, with around 150 rake vendors and 750 food stalls.
== Historical Development == During the late Edo period, the most famous Torinoichi was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in {{ill|Asakusa|ja|浅草|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, along with the adjacent {{ill|Chōkoku-ji (Taitō Ward)|lt=Chōkokuji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. These events remain prominent, drawing crowds from all over Tokyo.
==Shrines and Temples Known for the Cock Festival== {{see also|{{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}}} The Cock Festival, which rivals {{ill|Ebisu-kō|ja|えびす講|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as a festival wishing for business prosperity, is primarily celebrated in the {{ill|Kantō region|ja|関東地方|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, where it originated. Unlike the Ebisu-kō, which is widely practiced not only in the {{ill|Keihanshin|ja|京阪神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} area but also throughout both {{ill|Eastern Japan|ja|東日本|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Western Japan|ja|西日本|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the Cock Festival remains more localized around the Kantō region. Since the Meiji period, however, the festival has spread to some shrines and temples in {{ill|Hamamatsu|ja|浜松市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|ja|静岡県|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Toyohashi|ja|豊橋市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|ja|愛知県|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In recent years, it has even been celebrated at shrines in the {{ill|Nakamura-ku|ja|中村区|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Nagoya|ja|名古屋市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.<ref>At Susanoo Shrine in Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, the Cock Festival is held after enshrining deities from Ōtori Shrine as subsidiary deities. Other celebrations in the city, such as those at {{ill|Shichiji Temple|ja|稲園山七寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Ōsu Shichiji and Chōfukuji), are self-proclaimed Cock Festivals without clear historical connections to religious traditions.</ref>
The following are notable shrines and temples known for their Cock Festival celebrations. In addition to those listed, many other shrines in southern Kantō hold Cock Festivals (or rake markets): * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Adachi Ward, Tokyo) — The origin site of the Edo Cock Festival * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — One of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō, hosting Japan's largest Cock Festival, the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — Known as the "酉の寺" (Cock Temple) and the birthplace of the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|ja|花園神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Shinjuku Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the festival of a merged Ōtori Shrine and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|ja|大國魂神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Fuchū City, Tokyo) — The festival is hosted by its subsidiary shrine, Ōtori Shrine, and is one of the three major Cock Festivals in Kantō * {{ill|Nerima Ōtori Shrine|ja|練馬大鳥神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Nerima Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the Cock Festival every November on Cock Days, attracting tens of thousands of visitors * {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社|1=Washinomiya Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Kuki, Saitama Prefecture) — Considered the origin of the Great Cock Festival and hosts a smaller rake market * {{ill|Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|ja|熊野神社 (前橋市千代田町)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Maebashi, Gunma Prefecture) — Hosts the Maebashi Great Cock Festival, one of Maebashi's four major festivals * {{ill|Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|ja|金刀比羅・大鷲神社|1=Konpira and Ōtori Shrine|2=ja|3=金刀比羅・大鷲神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Yokohama, Kanagawa Prefecture) — Its Cock Festival is recognized as an intangible cultural property of Yokohama
Although the {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, is regarded as the head shrine of Ōtori faith, its "酉の日祭" (Cock Day Festival), held on the Cock Days in November,<ref>[http://www.ootoritaisha.jp/gyouji/ Ōtori Shrine official website]</ref> does not feature the rake markets or nighttime stalls typical of the Kantō region.
==Origin== The origin of the Cock Festival is explained differently by {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Buddhism|ja|仏教|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
=== Shinto Explanation === According to Shinto traditions, the Cock Festival originated from markets held on the day of the Great Cock Festival (Ōtori Matsuri). The deities of Ōtori Shrine (or Washi Shrine) include {{ill|Yamato Takeru|ja|ヤマトタケル|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, who prayed for victory during his eastern campaign at {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|ja|鷲宮神社|1=Washinomiya Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. He later celebrated his victory at the site of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Hanahata, which also commemorates the day of Yamato Takeru’s death. On November Cock Days (or December’s first Cock Day at Washinomiya Shrine), the Great Cock Festival is held. The shrine tradition of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa states that Yamato Takeru returned to give thanks on a November Cock Day and leaned his weapons against a pine tree in front of the shrine. This act led to the establishment of the Great Cock Festival and the use of decorative {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as auspicious items.
=== Buddhist Explanation === In Buddhist tradition, specifically at {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Asakusa, the Cock Festival originates from the market held during the unveiling (kaichō) of the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Washi Myōken Daibosatsu|ja|鷲妙見大菩薩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. On a November Cock Day in 1265 (Bun’ei 2), {{ill|Nichiren|ja|Nichiren|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|ja|Nichiren宗|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, was staying at the Kobayakawa household in {{ill|Kazusa Province|ja|上総国|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (present-day Mobara City, Chiba Prefecture). While praying for national peace, the morning star (Venus) shone brightly, and Washi Myōken Daibosatsu appeared riding on the back of an eagle. Since the establishment of Chōkoku-ji, the temple has held an annual market on November Cock Days, featuring the transfer of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu from Washiyama-dera. In 1771 (Meiwa 8), the statue of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu was enshrined permanently at Chōkoku-ji, where the annual Cock Festival continued.
=== Historical Practices === The festival is thought to have started as a harvest celebration by nearby farmers at the Hanahata Washi Daimyōjin shrine. Known also as the Rooster Daimyōjin, worshippers abstained from eating chicken meat, and even shrine families refrained from consuming eggs. Farmers offered live chickens as tributes, releasing them at the Asakusa Kannon Hall ({{ill|Sensō-ji|ja|浅草寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) after the festival.
Because the shrine was conveniently located along the Ayase River, it became a hub for people and goods transported via waterways. As a result, the Cock Day markets gradually attracted visitors from all over Edo (Tokyo). Gambling flourished at these markets until bans during the An’ei era curtailed the festivities.
Eventually, the thriving Cock Festival shifted to the Asakusa Washi Daimyōjin, which became the most prominent venue. Its proximity to {{ill|Yoshiwara|ja|吉原 (東京都)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a famous red-light district, further contributed to its popularity. Over time, Cock Festivals spread across Edo and are now celebrated at many shrines and temples in the Kantō region.
Thus, the Cock Festival evolved from a rural agricultural market showcasing autumn harvests and farming tools into an urban celebration featuring auspicious decorative rakes symbolizing good fortune and prosperity.
==Customs== [[File:酉の市Torinoichi002.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The Cock Festival at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. The shrine distributes auspicious {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.]]
=== Rake Talismans and Decorative Rakes === On the days of the Cock Festival, stalls line up selling "decorative rakes" (engimono kumade), adorned with items such as okame masks and other symbols of good fortune. Shrines hosting the festival also distribute small bamboo {{ill|rakes|ja|熊手|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, adorned with rice ears and talismans, as "rake talismans" (kumade mamori). These rakes are colloquially called "kakkome," a pun meaning to "sweep in" or "gather in" blessings. Originally, rakes and {{ill|hoes|ja|鍬|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, along with other farming tools, were sold to local farmers around Washi Shrine on festival days. Over time, auspicious items such as okame masks began to be attached to the tools as complimentary gifts, evolving into today's decorative rakes.<ref>[http://www.torinoichi.jp/goriyaku/goriyaku_5.html Cock Festival Benefits]</ref>
The Cock Festival's auspicious items have included "tou no imo" (唐の芋, a type of yam) and "kogane mochi" (黄金餅, millet cakes), since the Edo period. The yam symbolized advancement and promotion due to its "head" shape, while its numerous offspring represented fertility. The millet cakes were believed to bring wealth. However, from the late Edo period, {{ill|kirizansho|ja|切り山椒|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a type of sweet confection, replaced the millet cakes as a festival item. Eating kirizansho during this cold season is said to prevent colds.<ref>[http://www.otorisama.or.jp/mame.html About the Cock Festival]</ref>
The decorative rake is the festival's iconic auspicious item, symbolizing the talons of an {{ill|eagle|ja|鷲|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which "grasp" its prey. The rake thus conveys the idea of gathering fortune or seizing prosperity. Decorative rakes are often bought through lively bargaining exchanges between rake sellers and buyers, where victorious negotiations are celebrated with exuberant {{ill|tejime|ja|手締め|qq=draft|qq=draft}} hand clapping. The size of the decorative rakes tends to grow larger every year, reflecting sellers’ strategies and buyers’ desires for increasing fortune.
=== The Third Cock Day === The "Cock Day" (Tori no Hi) is determined using the {{ill|sexagenary cycle|ja|干支|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, occurring every twelve days.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/learning/elib/qa/qa_35.html |title=Is a Year with Three Cock Days More Prone to Fires? |access-date=2024-12-01 |publisher=Tokyo Fire Department}}</ref> Depending on the month’s alignment, November may have two or three Cock Days.<ref>For instance, if November 3 is the first Cock Day (Ichinotori), then November 15 will be the second (Ninotori), and November 27 the third (Sannotori). However, if November 8 is the first Cock Day, the second falls on November 20, and the next Cock Day occurs in December.</ref> The first Cock Day is called "Ichinotori," the second "Ninotori," and the third "Sannotori."
Years with three Cock Days are traditionally believed to have a higher incidence of fires, though there is no scientific basis for this claim.<ref name=":0" /> Consequently, in years with three Cock Days, greater care is taken with fire safety, especially in late December. Many rake merchants affix "Fire Safety" seals to their rakes during these years. Since three Cock Days occur approximately every other year, they are not particularly rare (see [[#List of Cock Days in November|List of Cock Days in November]]).
In Asakusa's {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a nearby {{ill|red-light district|ja|吉原 (東京都)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} called [[:en:Yoshiwara|Yoshiwara]] contributed to a peculiar custom. It is said that wives would warn their husbands about the fire risk of the third Cock Day to prevent them from visiting Yoshiwara under the pretense of attending the festival.<ref>[http://ii-nippon.net/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AE%E7%A5%AD/891.html Japanese Festivals: Three Popular Theories]</ref>
