<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Tori-no-ichi]][[ja:酉の市]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Tori-no-ichi]][[ja:酉の市]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[sn:commons:Category:Tori-no-ichi]][[ja:酉の市]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11643942]] Wikidata name: Tori no Ichi [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:01, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|{{ill|Torinoichi|ja|酉の市|1=Tori-no-Ichi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Torinoichi|13=User:Immanuelle/Tori-no-Ichi|qq=}} at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}}]] '''Torinoichi''' (酉の市) is a festival held annually on the [[:en:Rooster (zodiac)|Day of the Rooster]] in [[:en:November|November]]<ref>See {{anchor|List of "Days of the Rooster" in November|"Days of the Rooster" list}}.</ref>. It is also known as the '''Festival of the Rooster''' (酉の祭, Tori no Machi), '''Ōtori Festival''' (大酉祭, Ōtori Matsuri), or simply '''Otorisama''' (お酉様).
==Overview== [[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes at the [[:en:Hanazono Shrine|Hanazono Shrine]] in [[:en:Shinjuku|Shinjuku]], [[:en:Tokyo|Tokyo]], during the "酉の市" (Cock Festival).}]] [[File:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|[[:en:Hiroshige|Utagawa Hiroshige]]'s ''[[:en:One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo]],'' depicting the bustling visitors heading to {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} viewed from a brothel room in {{ill|Yoshiwara red-light district|ja|吉原遊廓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshiwara red-light district|qq=}}.<ref>The image echoes this scene with a hairpin in the bottom left shaped like a [[:en:Rake (tool)|good-luck rake]], decorated with suggestive elements such as {{ill|Okame|ja|おかめ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okame|1=Okame|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261405}} and matsutake mushrooms.</ref>]] [[File:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes during the "酉の市" at the subsidiary shrine [[:en:Ōkunitama Shrine|Ōtori Shrine (Fuchū)]].]]
The "酉の市" (Cock Festival) is an annual event associated with shrines and temples linked to roosters or birds, such as {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine|qq=}}, "酉の寺," and {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori taisha|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大鳥大社}}. Predominantly celebrated in the Kanto region, the festival is famous for its vibrant atmosphere, with many stalls selling [[:en:Rake (tool)|good-luck rakes]] amidst vigorous hand-clapping rituals. It is a well-known year-end tradition.
At {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine|qq=}}, which enshrines [[:en:Yamato Takeru|Yamato Takeru]], the deity is venerated as a patron of lasting military fortune, prosperity, and success in business. In the Kanto region, [[:en:Washinomiya Shrine|Washinomiya Shrine]] (in [[:en:Kuki, Saitama|Kuki]], [[:en:Saitama Prefecture|Saitama Prefecture]]) is regarded as the main shrine of Ōtori Shrines.<ref>In the [[:en:Kansai region|Kansai region]], [[:en:Ōtori taisha|Ōtori taisha]] (in [[:en:Sakai|Sakai]], [[:en:Osaka Prefecture|Osaka Prefecture]]) is considered the main shrine (M. Okada, "Guide to Famous Shrines Nationwide," published by Tokyo Daijingu). The connection between Ōtori shrines across Kanto remains unclear.</ref> The enshrined deities are {{ill|Ame-no-Hohi|ja|天穂日命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Hohi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to アメノホヒ|1=Ame no Hohi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10940685}}, {{ill|Takehi-Nateru|ja|武夷鳥命|fr|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takehi-Nateru|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 建比良鳥命}}, and {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōkuninushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大国主}}. Legend states that [[:en:Yamato Takeru|Yamato Takeru]] prayed for victory at the shrine during his eastern campaign. Over time, faith in "酉の日精進" (ritual abstinence on the Cock Day) spread, leading to the "大酉祭" (Great Cock Festival) held on the first Cock Day of December.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|qq=}} in {{ill|Hanahata Village|ja|花畑 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanahata Village|1=Hanahata|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11615595}}, [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]], became famous and was referred to as "本酉" (Main Cock). The harvest festival held by local residents around this shrine is considered the origin of the Edo Cock Festival. Currently, the shrine enshrines Yamato Takeru, who is said to have celebrated his victory at this location after returning from his campaign. During the Edo period, the shrine’s deity was identified as [[:en:The Buddha|Shakyamuni Tathāgata]], depicted riding on the back of a rooster. Historical records suggest that this festival dates back to the early 15th century during the [[:en:Ōei|Ōei era]]. Pilgrims offered roosters to pray for good fortune, later releasing them near [[:en:Sensō-ji|Sensō-ji]] in Asakusa after the festival ended.
By the late Edo period, the most prominent Cock Festival was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} and "酉の寺" {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}} in Asakusa. During this time, the deity at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine was considered the [[:en:Myōken|Myōken Bodhisattva]], riding on the back of a rooster. In Edo, the Cock Festivals were categorized as follows: the "上酉" (Upper Cock) or "本酉" (Main Cock) at Hanahata Ōtori Shrine, the "中酉" (Middle Cock) at {{ill|Shōsen-ji|ja|勝専寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōsen-ji|1=Shōsen-ji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q97202023}} in Senju, and the "下酉" (Lower Cock) or "新酉" (New Cock) at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji. By the late Edo period, Cock Festivals were also held at shrines like those in Sugamo and Zōshigaya. In the Meiji era, the Cock Festival at Senju’s Shōsen-ji ceased, but many traditions from the Edo period persist to this day.
Asakusa's Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji Temple were located next to {{ill|Shin-Yoshiwara|ja|新吉原|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shin-Yoshiwara|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 吉原 (東京都)|1=Yoshiwara|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1859550}}, a prominent red-light district. On festival days, the district would open its gates, adding to the popularity and renown of this Cock Festival. Today, it remains the largest Cock Festival in Japan, attracting approximately 70,000 to 80,000 visitors annually, with around 150 rake vendors and 750 food stalls.
== Historical Development == During the late Edo period, the most famous Torinoichi was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} in [[:en:Asakusa|Asakusa]], along with the adjacent {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|lt=Chōkokuji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}}. These events remain prominent, drawing crowds from all over Tokyo.
==Shrines and Temples Known for the Cock Festival== {{see also|{{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine|qq=}}}} The Cock Festival, which rivals {{ill|Ebisu-kō|ja|えびす講|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ebisu-kō|1=Ebisu-kō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261037}} as a festival wishing for business prosperity, is primarily celebrated in the [[:en:Kantō region|Kantō region]], where it originated. Unlike the Ebisu-kō, which is widely practiced not only in the [[:en:Keihanshin|Keihanshin]] area but also throughout both {{ill|Eastern Japan|ja|東日本|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eastern Japan|qq=}} and {{ill|Western Japan|ja|西日本|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Western Japan|1=Western Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1063946}}, the Cock Festival remains more localized around the Kantō region. Since the Meiji period, however, the festival has spread to some shrines and temples in [[:en:Hamamatsu|Hamamatsu]], [[:en:Shizuoka Prefecture|Shizuoka Prefecture]], and [[:en:Toyohashi|Toyohashi]], [[:en:Aichi Prefecture|Aichi Prefecture]]. In recent years, it has even been celebrated at shrines in the [[:en:Nakamura-ku, Nagoya|Nakamura-ku]], [[:en:Nagoya|Nagoya]].<ref>At Susanoo Shrine in Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, the Cock Festival is held after enshrining deities from Ōtori Shrine as subsidiary deities. Other celebrations in the city, such as those at {{ill|Shichiji Temple|ja|稲園山七寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shichiji Temple|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Ōsu Shichiji and Chōfukuji), are self-proclaimed Cock Festivals without clear historical connections to religious traditions.</ref>
The following are notable shrines and temples known for their Cock Festival celebrations. In addition to those listed, many other shrines in southern Kantō hold Cock Festivals (or rake markets): * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|qq=}} (Adachi Ward, Tokyo) — The origin site of the Edo Cock Festival * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — One of the three major Cock Festivals of Kantō, hosting Japan's largest Cock Festival, the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — Known as the "酉の寺" (Cock Temple) and the birthplace of the Asakusa Cock Festival * [[:en:Hanazono Shrine|Hanazono Shrine]] (Shinjuku Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the festival of a merged Ōtori Shrine and is one of the three major Cock Festivals of Kantō * [[:en:Ōkunitama Shrine|Ōkunitama Shrine]] (Fuchū City, Tokyo) — The festival is hosted by its subsidiary shrine, Ōtori Shrine, and is one of the three major Cock Festivals of Kantō * {{ill|Nerima Ōtori Shrine|ja|練馬大鳥神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nerima Ōtori Shrine|qq=}} (Nerima Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the Cock Festival every November on Cock Days, attracting tens of thousands of visitors * [[:en:Washinomiya Shrine|Washinomiya Shrine]] (Kuki, Saitama Prefecture) — Considered the origin of the Great Cock Festival and hosts a smaller rake market * {{ill|Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|ja|熊野神社 (前橋市千代田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Maebashi, Gunma Prefecture) — Hosts the Maebashi Great Cock Festival, one of Maebashi's four major festivals * {{ill|Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|ja|金刀比羅・大鷲神社|1=Konpira and Ōtori Shrine|2=ja|3=金刀比羅・大鷲神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|13=User:Immanuelle/Konpira and Ōtori Shrine|qq=}} (Yokohama, Kanagawa Prefecture) — Its Cock Festival is recognized as an intangible cultural property of Yokohama
Although the {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori taisha|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大鳥大社}} in Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, is regarded as the head shrine of Ōtori faith, its "酉の日祭" (Cock Day Festival), held on the Cock Days in November,<ref>[http://www.ootoritaisha.jp/gyouji/ Ōtori Shrine official website]</ref> does not feature the rake markets or nighttime stalls typical of the Kantō region.
==Origin== The origin of the Cock Festival is explained differently by [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] and [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]].
=== Shinto Explanation === According to Shinto traditions, the Cock Festival originated from markets held on the day of the Great Cock Festival (Ōtori Matsuri). The deities of Ōtori Shrine (or Washi Shrine) include [[:en:Yamato Takeru|Yamato Takeru]], who prayed for victory during his eastern campaign at [[:en:Washinomiya Shrine|Washinomiya Shrine]]. He later celebrated his victory at the site of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|qq=}} in Hanahata, which also commemorates the day of Yamato Takeru’s death. On November Cock Days (or December’s first Cock Day at Washinomiya Shrine), the Great Cock Festival is held. The shrine tradition of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} in Asakusa states that Yamato Takeru returned to give thanks on a November Cock Day and leaned his weapons against a pine tree in front of the shrine. This act led to the establishment of the Great Cock Festival and the use of decorative [[:en:Rake (tool)|rakes]] as auspicious items.
=== Buddhist Explanation === In Buddhist tradition, specifically at {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}} in Asakusa, the Cock Festival originates from the market held during the unveiling (kaichō) of the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Washi Myōken Daibosatsu|ja|鷲妙見大菩薩|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōken|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. On a November Cock Day in 1265 (Bun’ei 2), {{ill|Nichiren|ja|Nichiren|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nichiren|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|ja|Nichiren宗|1=Nichiren Shū|2=ja|3=日蓮宗|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nichiren Buddhism|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q206611}}, was staying at the Kobayakawa household in [[:en:Kazusa Province|Kazusa Province]] (present-day Mobara City, Chiba Prefecture). While praying for national peace, the morning star (Venus) shone brightly, and Washi Myōken Daibosatsu appeared riding on the back of an eagle. Since the establishment of Chōkoku-ji, the temple has held an annual market on November Cock Days, featuring the transfer of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu from Washiyama-dera. In 1771 (Meiwa 8), the statue of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu was enshrined permanently at Chōkoku-ji, where the annual Cock Festival continued.
=== Historical Practices === The festival is thought to have started as a harvest celebration by nearby farmers at the Hanahata Washi Daimyōjin shrine. Known also as the Rooster Daimyōjin, worshippers abstained from eating chicken meat, and even shrine families refrained from consuming eggs. Farmers offered live chickens as tributes, releasing them at the Asakusa Kannon Hall ([[:en:Sensō-ji|Sensō-ji]]) after the festival.
Because the shrine was conveniently located along the Ayase River, it became a hub for people and goods transported via waterways. As a result, the Cock Day markets gradually attracted visitors from all over Edo (Tokyo). Gambling flourished at these markets until bans during the An’ei era curtailed the festivities.
Eventually, the thriving Cock Festival shifted to the Asakusa Washi Daimyōjin, which became the most prominent venue. Its proximity to [[:en:Yoshiwara|Yoshiwara]], a famous red-light district, further contributed to its popularity. Over time, Cock Festivals spread across Edo and are now celebrated at many shrines and temples in the Kantō region.
Thus, the Cock Festival evolved from a rural agricultural market showcasing autumn harvests and farming tools into an urban celebration featuring auspicious decorative rakes symbolizing good fortune and prosperity.
==Customs== [[File:酉の市Torinoichi002.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The Cock Festival at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|qq=}}. The shrine distributes auspicious [[:en:Rake (tool)|rakes]].]]
=== Rake Talismans and Decorative Rakes === On the days of the Cock Festival, stalls line up selling "decorative rakes" (engimono kumade), adorned with items such as okame masks and other symbols of good fortune. Shrines hosting the festival also distribute small bamboo [[:en:Rake (tool)|rakes]], adorned with rice ears and talismans, as "rake talismans" (kumade mamori). These rakes are colloquially called "kakkome," a pun meaning to "sweep in" or "gather in" blessings. Originally, rakes and [[:en:Hoe (tool)|hoes]], along with other farming tools, were sold to local farmers around Washi Shrine on festival days. Over time, auspicious items such as okame masks began to be attached to the tools as complimentary gifts, evolving into today's decorative rakes.<ref>[http://www.torinoichi.jp/goriyaku/goriyaku_5.html Cock Festival Benefits]</ref>
The Cock Festival's auspicious items have included "tou no imo" (唐の芋, a type of yam) and "kogane mochi" (黄金餅, millet cakes), since the Edo period. The yam symbolized advancement and promotion due to its "head" shape, while its numerous offspring represented fertility. The millet cakes were believed to bring wealth. However, from the late Edo period, {{ill|kirizansho|ja|切り山椒|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/kirizansho|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 切山椒}}, a type of sweet confection, replaced the millet cakes as a festival item. Eating kirizansho during this cold season is said to prevent colds.<ref>[http://www.otorisama.or.jp/mame.html About the Cock Festival]</ref>
The decorative rake is the festival's iconic auspicious item, symbolizing the talons of an [[:en:Eagle|eagle]], which "grasp" its prey. The rake thus conveys the idea of gathering fortune or seizing prosperity. Decorative rakes are often bought through lively bargaining exchanges between rake sellers and buyers, where victorious negotiations are celebrated with exuberant [[:en:Tejime|tejime]] hand clapping. The size of the decorative rakes tends to grow larger every year, reflecting sellers’ strategies and buyers’ desires for increasing fortune.
=== The Third Cock Day === The "Cock Day" (Tori no Hi) is determined using the [[:en:Sexagenary cycle|sexagenary cycle]], occurring every twelve days.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/learning/elib/qa/qa_35.html |title=Is a Year with Three Cock Days More Prone to Fires? |access-date=2024-12-01 |publisher=Tokyo Fire Department}}</ref> Depending on the month’s alignment, November may have two or three Cock Days.<ref>For instance, if November 3 is the first Cock Day (Ichinotori), then November 15 will be the second (Ninotori), and November 27 the third (Sannotori). However, if November 8 is the first Cock Day, the second falls on November 20, and the next Cock Day occurs in December.</ref> The first Cock Day is called "Ichinotori," the second "Ninotori," and the third "Sannotori."
Years with three Cock Days are traditionally believed to have a higher incidence of fires, though there is no scientific basis for this claim.<ref name=":0" /> Consequently, in years with three Cock Days, greater care is taken with fire safety, especially in late December. Many rake merchants affix "Fire Safety" seals to their rakes during these years. Since three Cock Days occur approximately every other year, they are not particularly rare (see [[#List of Cock Days in November|List of Cock Days in November]]).
In Asakusa's {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} and {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}}, a nearby [[:en:Yoshiwara|red-light district]] called [[:en:Yoshiwara|Yoshiwara]] contributed to a peculiar custom. It is said that wives would warn their husbands about the fire risk of the third Cock Day to prevent them from visiting Yoshiwara under the pretense of attending the festival.<ref>[http://ii-nippon.net/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AE%E7%A5%AD/891.html Japanese Festivals: Three Popular Theories]</ref>
<gallery> File:Shinto worships at Cock Festival of Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|Scene from the Cock Festival at [[:en:Hanazono Shrine|Hanazono Shrine]] File:酉の市Torinoichi000.jpg|A large decorative rake at [[:en:Ōkunitama Shrine|Ōkunitama Shrine]] File:酉の市Torinoichi005.jpg|Bustling scene at the Cock Festival File:酉の市Torinoichi003.jpg|Vendors selling rakes at stalls File:Kirizansho.jpg|{{ill|Kirizansho|ja|切り山椒|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kirizansho|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 切山椒}}, a festival confection </gallery>

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Tori-no-ichi]][[ja:酉の市]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Tori-no-ichi]][[ja:酉の市]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[sn:commons:Category:Tori-no-ichi]][[ja:酉の市]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11643942]] Wikidata name: Tori no Ichi [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:01, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|{{ill|Torinoichi|ja|酉の市|1=Tori-no-Ichi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Torinoichi|13=User:Immanuelle/Tori-no-Ichi|qq=}} at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}}]] '''Torinoichi''' (酉の市) is a festival held annually on the {{ill|Rooster (zodiac)|en|Rooster (zodiac)|WD=Q822621|lt=Day of the Rooster}} in {{ill|November|en|November|WD=Q125|lt=November}}<ref>See {{anchor|List of "Days of the Rooster" in November|"Days of the Rooster" list}}.</ref>. It is also known as the '''Festival of the Rooster''' (酉の祭, Tori no Machi), '''Ōtori Festival''' (大酉祭, Ōtori Matsuri), or simply '''Otorisama''' (お酉様).
==Overview== [[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes at the {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en|Hanazono Shrine|WD=Q3126680|lt=Hanazono Shrine}} in {{ill|Shinjuku|en|Shinjuku|WD=Q179645|lt=Shinjuku}}, {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo}}, during the "酉の市" (Cock Festival).}]] [[File:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|{{ill|Hiroshige|en|Hiroshige|WD=Q200798|lt=Utagawa Hiroshige}}'s ''{{ill|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|en|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|WD=Q165190|lt=One Hundred Famous Views of Edo}},'' depicting the bustling visitors heading to {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} viewed from a brothel room in {{ill|Yoshiwara red-light district|ja|吉原遊廓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshiwara red-light district|qq=}}.<ref>The image echoes this scene with a hairpin in the bottom left shaped like a {{ill|Rake (tool)|en|Rake (tool)|WD=Q200822|lt=good-luck rake}}, decorated with suggestive elements such as {{ill|Okame|ja|おかめ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okame|1=Okame|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261405}} and matsutake mushrooms.</ref>]] [[File:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes during the "酉の市" at the subsidiary shrine {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|en|Ōkunitama Shrine|WD=Q611678|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Fuchū)}}.]]
The "酉の市" (Cock Festival) is an annual event associated with shrines and temples linked to roosters or birds, such as {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine|qq=}}, "酉の寺," and {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori taisha|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大鳥大社}}. Predominantly celebrated in the Kanto region, the festival is famous for its vibrant atmosphere, with many stalls selling {{ill|Rake (tool)|en|Rake (tool)|WD=Q200822|lt=good-luck rakes}} amidst vigorous hand-clapping rituals. It is a well-known year-end tradition.
At {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine|qq=}}, which enshrines {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}}, the deity is venerated as a patron of lasting military fortune, prosperity, and success in business. In the Kanto region, {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en|Washinomiya Shrine|WD=Q611108|lt=Washinomiya Shrine}} (in {{ill|Kuki, Saitama|en|Kuki, Saitama|WD=Q47535|lt=Kuki}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|en|Saitama Prefecture|WD=Q128186|lt=Saitama Prefecture}}) is regarded as the main shrine of Ōtori Shrines.<ref>In the {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kansai region}}, {{ill|Ōtori taisha|en|Ōtori taisha|WD=Q705151|lt=Ōtori taisha}} (in {{ill|Sakai|en|Sakai|WD=Q193428|lt=Sakai}}, {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en|Osaka Prefecture|WD=Q122723|lt=Osaka Prefecture}}) is considered the main shrine (M. Okada, "Guide to Famous Shrines Nationwide," published by Tokyo Daijingu). The connection between Ōtori shrines across Kanto remains unclear.</ref> The enshrined deities are {{ill|Ame-no-Hohi|ja|天穂日命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Hohi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to アメノホヒ|1=Ame no Hohi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10940685}}, {{ill|Takehi-Nateru|ja|武夷鳥命|fr|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takehi-Nateru|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 建比良鳥命}}, and {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōkuninushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大国主}}. Legend states that {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}} prayed for victory at the shrine during his eastern campaign. Over time, faith in "酉の日精進" (ritual abstinence on the Cock Day) spread, leading to the "大酉祭" (Great Cock Festival) held on the first Cock Day of December.
In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|qq=}} in {{ill|Hanahata Village|ja|花畑 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanahata Village|1=Hanahata|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11615595}}, {{ill|Musashi Province|en|Musashi Province|WD=Q907398|lt=Musashi Province}}, became famous and was referred to as "本酉" (Main Cock). The harvest festival held by local residents around this shrine is considered the origin of the Edo Cock Festival. Currently, the shrine enshrines Yamato Takeru, who is said to have celebrated his victory at this location after returning from his campaign. During the Edo period, the shrine’s deity was identified as {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=Shakyamuni Tathāgata}}, depicted riding on the back of a rooster. Historical records suggest that this festival dates back to the early 15th century during the {{ill|Ōei|en|Ōei|WD=Q1193078|lt=Ōei era}}. Pilgrims offered roosters to pray for good fortune, later releasing them near {{ill|Sensō-ji|en|Sensō-ji|WD=Q615183|lt=Sensō-ji}} in Asakusa after the festival ended.
By the late Edo period, the most prominent Cock Festival was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} and "酉の寺" {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}} in Asakusa. During this time, the deity at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine was considered the {{ill|Myōken|en|Myōken|WD=Q10960623|lt=Myōken Bodhisattva}}, riding on the back of a rooster. In Edo, the Cock Festivals were categorized as follows: the "上酉" (Upper Cock) or "本酉" (Main Cock) at Hanahata Ōtori Shrine, the "中酉" (Middle Cock) at {{ill|Shōsen-ji|ja|勝専寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōsen-ji|1=Shōsen-ji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q97202023}} in Senju, and the "下酉" (Lower Cock) or "新酉" (New Cock) at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji. By the late Edo period, Cock Festivals were also held at shrines like those in Sugamo and Zōshigaya. In the Meiji era, the Cock Festival at Senju’s Shōsen-ji ceased, but many traditions from the Edo period persist to this day.
Asakusa's Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji Temple were located next to {{ill|Shin-Yoshiwara|ja|新吉原|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shin-Yoshiwara|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 吉原 (東京都)|1=Yoshiwara|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1859550}}, a prominent red-light district. On festival days, the district would open its gates, adding to the popularity and renown of this Cock Festival. Today, it remains the largest Cock Festival in Japan, attracting approximately 70,000 to 80,000 visitors annually, with around 150 rake vendors and 750 food stalls.
== Historical Development == During the late Edo period, the most famous Torinoichi was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} in {{ill|Asakusa|en|Asakusa|WD=Q720644|lt=Asakusa}}, along with the adjacent {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|lt=Chōkokuji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}}. These events remain prominent, drawing crowds from all over Tokyo.
==Shrines and Temples Known for the Cock Festival== {{see also|{{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine|qq=}}}} The Cock Festival, which rivals {{ill|Ebisu-kō|ja|えびす講|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ebisu-kō|1=Ebisu-kō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261037}} as a festival wishing for business prosperity, is primarily celebrated in the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|WD=Q132480|lt=Kantō region}}, where it originated. Unlike the Ebisu-kō, which is widely practiced not only in the {{ill|Keihanshin|en|Keihanshin|WD=Q1149484|lt=Keihanshin}} area but also throughout both {{ill|Eastern Japan|ja|東日本|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eastern Japan|qq=}} and {{ill|Western Japan|ja|西日本|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Western Japan|1=Western Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1063946}}, the Cock Festival remains more localized around the Kantō region. Since the Meiji period, however, the festival has spread to some shrines and temples in {{ill|Hamamatsu|en|Hamamatsu|WD=Q185125|lt=Hamamatsu}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}, and {{ill|Toyohashi|en|Toyohashi|WD=Q336431|lt=Toyohashi}}, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|WD=Q80434|lt=Aichi Prefecture}}. In recent years, it has even been celebrated at shrines in the {{ill|Nakamura-ku, Nagoya|en|Nakamura-ku, Nagoya|WD=Q780521|lt=Nakamura-ku}}, {{ill|Nagoya|en|Nagoya|WD=Q11751|lt=Nagoya}}.<ref>At Susanoo Shrine in Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, the Cock Festival is held after enshrining deities from Ōtori Shrine as subsidiary deities. Other celebrations in the city, such as those at {{ill|Shichiji Temple|ja|稲園山七寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shichiji Temple|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Ōsu Shichiji and Chōfukuji), are self-proclaimed Cock Festivals without clear historical connections to religious traditions.</ref>
The following are notable shrines and temples known for their Cock Festival celebrations. In addition to those listed, many other shrines in southern Kantō hold Cock Festivals (or rake markets): * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|qq=}} (Adachi Ward, Tokyo) — The origin site of the Edo Cock Festival * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — One of the three major Cock Festivals of Kantō, hosting Japan's largest Cock Festival, the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — Known as the "酉の寺" (Cock Temple) and the birthplace of the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en|Hanazono Shrine|WD=Q3126680|lt=Hanazono Shrine}} (Shinjuku Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the festival of a merged Ōtori Shrine and is one of the three major Cock Festivals of Kantō * {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|en|Ōkunitama Shrine|WD=Q611678|lt=Ōkunitama Shrine}} (Fuchū City, Tokyo) — The festival is hosted by its subsidiary shrine, Ōtori Shrine, and is one of the three major Cock Festivals of Kantō * {{ill|Nerima Ōtori Shrine|ja|練馬大鳥神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nerima Ōtori Shrine|qq=}} (Nerima Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the Cock Festival every November on Cock Days, attracting tens of thousands of visitors * {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en|Washinomiya Shrine|WD=Q611108|lt=Washinomiya Shrine}} (Kuki, Saitama Prefecture) — Considered the origin of the Great Cock Festival and hosts a smaller rake market * {{ill|Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|ja|熊野神社 (前橋市千代田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Maebashi, Gunma Prefecture) — Hosts the Maebashi Great Cock Festival, one of Maebashi's four major festivals * {{ill|Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|ja|金刀比羅・大鷲神社|1=Konpira and Ōtori Shrine|2=ja|3=金刀比羅・大鷲神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|13=User:Immanuelle/Konpira and Ōtori Shrine|qq=}} (Yokohama, Kanagawa Prefecture) — Its Cock Festival is recognized as an intangible cultural property of Yokohama
Although the {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori taisha|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大鳥大社}} in Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, is regarded as the head shrine of Ōtori faith, its "酉の日祭" (Cock Day Festival), held on the Cock Days in November,<ref>[http://www.ootoritaisha.jp/gyouji/ Ōtori Shrine official website]</ref> does not feature the rake markets or nighttime stalls typical of the Kantō region.
==Origin== The origin of the Cock Festival is explained differently by {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|WD=Q812767|lt=Shinto}} and {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}}.
=== Shinto Explanation === According to Shinto traditions, the Cock Festival originated from markets held on the day of the Great Cock Festival (Ōtori Matsuri). The deities of Ōtori Shrine (or Washi Shrine) include {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}}, who prayed for victory during his eastern campaign at {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en|Washinomiya Shrine|WD=Q611108|lt=Washinomiya Shrine}}. He later celebrated his victory at the site of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|qq=}} in Hanahata, which also commemorates the day of Yamato Takeru’s death. On November Cock Days (or December’s first Cock Day at Washinomiya Shrine), the Great Cock Festival is held. The shrine tradition of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} in Asakusa states that Yamato Takeru returned to give thanks on a November Cock Day and leaned his weapons against a pine tree in front of the shrine. This act led to the establishment of the Great Cock Festival and the use of decorative {{ill|Rake (tool)|en|Rake (tool)|WD=Q200822|lt=rakes}} as auspicious items.
=== Buddhist Explanation === In Buddhist tradition, specifically at {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}} in Asakusa, the Cock Festival originates from the market held during the unveiling (kaichō) of the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Washi Myōken Daibosatsu|ja|鷲妙見大菩薩|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōken|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. On a November Cock Day in 1265 (Bun’ei 2), {{ill|Nichiren|ja|Nichiren|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nichiren|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|ja|Nichiren宗|1=Nichiren Shū|2=ja|3=日蓮宗|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nichiren Buddhism|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q206611}}, was staying at the Kobayakawa household in {{ill|Kazusa Province|en|Kazusa Province|WD=Q1055394|lt=Kazusa Province}} (present-day Mobara City, Chiba Prefecture). While praying for national peace, the morning star (Venus) shone brightly, and Washi Myōken Daibosatsu appeared riding on the back of an eagle. Since the establishment of Chōkoku-ji, the temple has held an annual market on November Cock Days, featuring the transfer of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu from Washiyama-dera. In 1771 (Meiwa 8), the statue of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu was enshrined permanently at Chōkoku-ji, where the annual Cock Festival continued.
=== Historical Practices === The festival is thought to have started as a harvest celebration by nearby farmers at the Hanahata Washi Daimyōjin shrine. Known also as the Rooster Daimyōjin, worshippers abstained from eating chicken meat, and even shrine families refrained from consuming eggs. Farmers offered live chickens as tributes, releasing them at the Asakusa Kannon Hall ({{ill|Sensō-ji|en|Sensō-ji|WD=Q615183|lt=Sensō-ji}}) after the festival.
Because the shrine was conveniently located along the Ayase River, it became a hub for people and goods transported via waterways. As a result, the Cock Day markets gradually attracted visitors from all over Edo (Tokyo). Gambling flourished at these markets until bans during the An’ei era curtailed the festivities.
Eventually, the thriving Cock Festival shifted to the Asakusa Washi Daimyōjin, which became the most prominent venue. Its proximity to {{ill|Yoshiwara|en|Yoshiwara|WD=Q1859550|lt=Yoshiwara}}, a famous red-light district, further contributed to its popularity. Over time, Cock Festivals spread across Edo and are now celebrated at many shrines and temples in the Kantō region.
Thus, the Cock Festival evolved from a rural agricultural market showcasing autumn harvests and farming tools into an urban celebration featuring auspicious decorative rakes symbolizing good fortune and prosperity.
==Customs== [[File:酉の市Torinoichi002.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The Cock Festival at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|qq=}}. The shrine distributes auspicious {{ill|Rake (tool)|en|Rake (tool)|WD=Q200822|lt=rakes}}.]]
=== Rake Talismans and Decorative Rakes === On the days of the Cock Festival, stalls line up selling "decorative rakes" (engimono kumade), adorned with items such as okame masks and other symbols of good fortune. Shrines hosting the festival also distribute small bamboo {{ill|Rake (tool)|en|Rake (tool)|WD=Q200822|lt=rakes}}, adorned with rice ears and talismans, as "rake talismans" (kumade mamori). These rakes are colloquially called "kakkome," a pun meaning to "sweep in" or "gather in" blessings. Originally, rakes and {{ill|Hoe (tool)|en|Hoe (tool)|WD=Q131154|lt=hoes}}, along with other farming tools, were sold to local farmers around Washi Shrine on festival days. Over time, auspicious items such as okame masks began to be attached to the tools as complimentary gifts, evolving into today's decorative rakes.<ref>[http://www.torinoichi.jp/goriyaku/goriyaku_5.html Cock Festival Benefits]</ref>
The Cock Festival's auspicious items have included "tou no imo" (唐の芋, a type of yam) and "kogane mochi" (黄金餅, millet cakes), since the Edo period. The yam symbolized advancement and promotion due to its "head" shape, while its numerous offspring represented fertility. The millet cakes were believed to bring wealth. However, from the late Edo period, {{ill|kirizansho|ja|切り山椒|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/kirizansho|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 切山椒}}, a type of sweet confection, replaced the millet cakes as a festival item. Eating kirizansho during this cold season is said to prevent colds.<ref>[http://www.otorisama.or.jp/mame.html About the Cock Festival]</ref>
The decorative rake is the festival's iconic auspicious item, symbolizing the talons of an {{ill|Eagle|en|Eagle|WD=Q2092297|lt=eagle}}, which "grasp" its prey. The rake thus conveys the idea of gathering fortune or seizing prosperity. Decorative rakes are often bought through lively bargaining exchanges between rake sellers and buyers, where victorious negotiations are celebrated with exuberant {{ill|Tejime|en|Tejime|WD=Q3982616|lt=tejime}} hand clapping. The size of the decorative rakes tends to grow larger every year, reflecting sellers’ strategies and buyers’ desires for increasing fortune.
=== The Third Cock Day === The "Cock Day" (Tori no Hi) is determined using the {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=sexagenary cycle}}, occurring every twelve days.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/learning/elib/qa/qa_35.html |title=Is a Year with Three Cock Days More Prone to Fires? |access-date=2024-12-01 |publisher=Tokyo Fire Department}}</ref> Depending on the month’s alignment, November may have two or three Cock Days.<ref>For instance, if November 3 is the first Cock Day (Ichinotori), then November 15 will be the second (Ninotori), and November 27 the third (Sannotori). However, if November 8 is the first Cock Day, the second falls on November 20, and the next Cock Day occurs in December.</ref> The first Cock Day is called "Ichinotori," the second "Ninotori," and the third "Sannotori."
Years with three Cock Days are traditionally believed to have a higher incidence of fires, though there is no scientific basis for this claim.<ref name=":0" /> Consequently, in years with three Cock Days, greater care is taken with fire safety, especially in late December. Many rake merchants affix "Fire Safety" seals to their rakes during these years. Since three Cock Days occur approximately every other year, they are not particularly rare (see [[#List of Cock Days in November|List of Cock Days in November]]).
In Asakusa's {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} and {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}}, a nearby {{ill|Yoshiwara|en|Yoshiwara|WD=Q1859550|lt=red-light district}} called {{ill|Yoshiwara|en|Yoshiwara|WD=Q1859550|lt=Yoshiwara}} contributed to a peculiar custom. It is said that wives would warn their husbands about the fire risk of the third Cock Day to prevent them from visiting Yoshiwara under the pretense of attending the festival.<ref>[http://ii-nippon.net/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AE%E7%A5%AD/891.html Japanese Festivals: Three Popular Theories]</ref>
<gallery> File:Shinto worships at Cock Festival of Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|Scene from the Cock Festival at {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en|Hanazono Shrine|WD=Q3126680|lt=Hanazono Shrine}} File:酉の市Torinoichi000.jpg|A large decorative rake at {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|en|Ōkunitama Shrine|WD=Q611678|lt=Ōkunitama Shrine}} File:酉の市Torinoichi005.jpg|Bustling scene at the Cock Festival File:酉の市Torinoichi003.jpg|Vendors selling rakes at stalls File:Kirizansho.jpg|{{ill|Kirizansho|ja|切り山椒|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kirizansho|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 切山椒}}, a festival confection </gallery>

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Tori-no-ichi]][[ja:酉の市]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[co:commons:Category:Tori-no-ichi]][[ja:酉の市]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[sn:commons:Category:Tori-no-ichi]][[ja:酉の市]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11643942]] Wikidata name: Tori no Ichi [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:01, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:鷲神社.jpg|thumb|300px|{{ill|Torinoichi|ja|酉の市|1=Tori-no-Ichi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Torinoichi|13=User:Immanuelle/Tori-no-Ichi|qq=}} at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}}]] '''Torinoichi''' (酉の市) is a festival held annually on the {{ill|Rooster (zodiac)|en|Rooster (zodiac)|WD=Q822621|lt=Day of the Rooster}} in {{ill|November|en|November|WD=Q125|lt=November}}<ref>See {{anchor|List of "Days of the Rooster" in November|"Days of the Rooster" list}}.</ref>. It is also known as the '''Festival of the Rooster''' (酉の祭, Tori no Machi), '''Ōtori Festival''' (大酉祭, Ōtori Matsuri), or simply '''Otorisama''' (お酉様).
==Overview== [[File:Cock Festival at Hanazono Shrine in Japan.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes at the {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en|Hanazono Shrine|WD=Q3126680|lt=Hanazono Shrine}} in {{ill|Shinjuku|en|Shinjuku|WD=Q179645|lt=Shinjuku}}, {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo}}, during the "酉の市" (Cock Festival).}]] [[File:100 views edo 101.jpg|thumb|240px|{{ill|Hiroshige|en|Hiroshige|WD=Q200798|lt=Utagawa Hiroshige}}'s ''{{ill|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|en|One Hundred Famous Views of Edo|WD=Q165190|lt=One Hundred Famous Views of Edo}},'' depicting the bustling visitors heading to {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} viewed from a brothel room in {{ill|Yoshiwara red-light district|ja|吉原遊廓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshiwara red-light district|qq=}}.<ref>The image echoes this scene with a hairpin in the bottom left shaped like a {{ill|Rake (tool)|en|Rake (tool)|WD=Q200822|lt=good-luck rake}}, decorated with suggestive elements such as {{ill|Okame|ja|おかめ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okame|1=Okame|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261405}} and matsutake mushrooms.</ref>]] [[File:酉の市Torinoichi004.jpg|thumb|240px|A stall selling good-luck rakes during the "酉の市" at the subsidiary shrine {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|en|Ōkunitama Shrine|WD=Q611678|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Fuchū)}}.]]
The "酉の市" (Cock Festival) is an annual event associated with shrines and temples linked to roosters or birds, such as {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine|qq=}}, "酉の寺," and {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori taisha|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大鳥大社}}. Predominantly celebrated in the Kanto region, the festival is famous for its vibrant atmosphere, with many stalls selling {{ill|Rake (tool)|en|Rake (tool)|WD=Q200822|lt=good-luck rakes}} amidst vigorous hand-clapping rituals. It is a well-known year-end tradition.
At {{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine|qq=}}, which enshrines {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}}, the deity is venerated as a patron of lasting military fortune, prosperity, and success in business. In the Kanto region, {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en|Washinomiya Shrine|WD=Q611108|lt=Washinomiya Shrine}} (in {{ill|Kuki, Saitama|en|Kuki, Saitama|WD=Q47535|lt=Kuki}}, {{ill|Saitama Prefecture|en|Saitama Prefecture|WD=Q128186|lt=Saitama Prefecture}}) is regarded as the main shrine of Ōtori Shrines.<ref>In the {{ill|Kansai region|en|Kansai region|WD=Q164256|lt=Kansai region}}, {{ill|Ōtori taisha|en|Ōtori taisha|WD=Q705151|lt=Ōtori taisha}} (in {{ill|Sakai|en|Sakai|WD=Q193428|lt=Sakai}}, {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en|Osaka Prefecture|WD=Q122723|lt=Osaka Prefecture}}) is considered the main shrine (M. Okada, "Guide to Famous Shrines Nationwide," published by Tokyo Daijingu). The connection between Ōtori shrines across Kanto remains unclear.</ref> The enshrined deities are {{ill|Ame-no-Hohi|ja|天穂日命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Hohi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to アメノホヒ|1=Ame no Hohi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10940685}}, {{ill|Takehi-Nateru|ja|武夷鳥命|fr|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takehi-Nateru|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 建比良鳥命}}, and {{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大己貴命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōkuninushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大国主}}. Legend states that {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}} prayed for victory at the shrine during his eastern campaign. Over time, faith in "酉の日精進" (ritual abstinence on the Cock Day) spread, leading to the "大酉祭" (Great Cock Festival) held on the first Cock Day of December.
In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|qq=}} in {{ill|Hanahata Village|ja|花畑 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanahata Village|1=Hanahata|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11615595}}, {{ill|Musashi Province|en|Musashi Province|WD=Q907398|lt=Musashi Province}}, became famous and was referred to as "本酉" (Main Cock). The harvest festival held by local residents around this shrine is considered the origin of the Edo Cock Festival. Currently, the shrine enshrines Yamato Takeru, who is said to have celebrated his victory at this location after returning from his campaign. During the Edo period, the shrine’s deity was identified as {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=Shakyamuni Tathāgata}}, depicted riding on the back of a rooster. Historical records suggest that this festival dates back to the early 15th century during the {{ill|Ōei|en|Ōei|WD=Q1193078|lt=Ōei era}}. Pilgrims offered roosters to pray for good fortune, later releasing them near {{ill|Sensō-ji|en|Sensō-ji|WD=Q615183|lt=Sensō-ji}} in Asakusa after the festival ended.
By the late Edo period, the most prominent Cock Festival was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} and "酉の寺" {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}} in Asakusa. During this time, the deity at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine was considered the {{ill|Myōken|en|Myōken|WD=Q10960623|lt=Myōken Bodhisattva}}, riding on the back of a rooster. In Edo, the Cock Festivals were categorized as follows: the "上酉" (Upper Cock) or "本酉" (Main Cock) at Hanahata Ōtori Shrine, the "中酉" (Middle Cock) at {{ill|Shōsen-ji|ja|勝専寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōsen-ji|1=Shōsen-ji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q97202023}} in Senju, and the "下酉" (Lower Cock) or "新酉" (New Cock) at Asakusa Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji. By the late Edo period, Cock Festivals were also held at shrines like those in Sugamo and Zōshigaya. In the Meiji era, the Cock Festival at Senju’s Shōsen-ji ceased, but many traditions from the Edo period persist to this day.
Asakusa's Ōtori Shrine and Chōkoku-ji Temple were located next to {{ill|Shin-Yoshiwara|ja|新吉原|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shin-Yoshiwara|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 吉原 (東京都)|1=Yoshiwara|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1859550}}, a prominent red-light district. On festival days, the district would open its gates, adding to the popularity and renown of this Cock Festival. Today, it remains the largest Cock Festival in Japan, attracting approximately 70,000 to 80,000 visitors annually, with around 150 rake vendors and 750 food stalls.
== Historical Development == During the late Edo period, the most famous Torinoichi was held at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} in {{ill|Asakusa|en|Asakusa|WD=Q720644|lt=Asakusa}}, along with the adjacent {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|lt=Chōkokuji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}}. These events remain prominent, drawing crowds from all over Tokyo.
==Shrines and Temples Known for the Cock Festival== {{see also|{{ill|Ōtori Shrine|ja|鷲神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine|qq=}}}} The Cock Festival, which rivals {{ill|Ebisu-kō|ja|えびす講|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ebisu-kō|1=Ebisu-kō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11261037}} as a festival wishing for business prosperity, is primarily celebrated in the {{ill|Kantō region|en|Kantō region|WD=Q132480|lt=Kantō region}}, where it originated. Unlike the Ebisu-kō, which is widely practiced not only in the {{ill|Keihanshin|en|Keihanshin|WD=Q1149484|lt=Keihanshin}} area but also throughout both {{ill|Eastern Japan|ja|東日本|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eastern Japan|qq=}} and {{ill|Western Japan|ja|西日本|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Western Japan|1=Western Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1063946}}, the Cock Festival remains more localized around the Kantō region. Since the Meiji period, however, the festival has spread to some shrines and temples in {{ill|Hamamatsu|en|Hamamatsu|WD=Q185125|lt=Hamamatsu}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|en|Shizuoka Prefecture|WD=Q131320|lt=Shizuoka Prefecture}}, and {{ill|Toyohashi|en|Toyohashi|WD=Q336431|lt=Toyohashi}}, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|WD=Q80434|lt=Aichi Prefecture}}. In recent years, it has even been celebrated at shrines in the {{ill|Nakamura-ku, Nagoya|en|Nakamura-ku, Nagoya|WD=Q780521|lt=Nakamura-ku}}, {{ill|Nagoya|en|Nagoya|WD=Q11751|lt=Nagoya}}.<ref>At Susanoo Shrine in Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, the Cock Festival is held after enshrining deities from Ōtori Shrine as subsidiary deities. Other celebrations in the city, such as those at {{ill|Shichiji Temple|ja|稲園山七寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shichiji Temple|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Ōsu Shichiji and Chōfukuji), are self-proclaimed Cock Festivals without clear historical connections to religious traditions.</ref>
The following are notable shrines and temples known for their Cock Festival celebrations. In addition to those listed, many other shrines in southern Kantō hold Cock Festivals (or rake markets): * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|qq=}} (Adachi Ward, Tokyo) — The origin site of the Edo Cock Festival * {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — One of the three major Cock Festivals of Kantō, hosting Japan's largest Cock Festival, the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}} (Taitō Ward, Tokyo) — Known as the "酉の寺" (Cock Temple) and the birthplace of the Asakusa Cock Festival * {{ill|Hanazono Shrine|en|Hanazono Shrine|WD=Q3126680|lt=Hanazono Shrine}} (Shinjuku Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the festival of a merged Ōtori Shrine and is one of the three major Cock Festivals of Kantō * {{ill|Ōkunitama Shrine|en|Ōkunitama Shrine|WD=Q611678|lt=Ōkunitama Shrine}} (Fuchū City, Tokyo) — The festival is hosted by its subsidiary shrine, Ōtori Shrine, and is one of the three major Cock Festivals of Kantō * {{ill|Nerima Ōtori Shrine|ja|練馬大鳥神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nerima Ōtori Shrine|qq=}} (Nerima Ward, Tokyo) — Hosts the Cock Festival every November on Cock Days, attracting tens of thousands of visitors * {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en|Washinomiya Shrine|WD=Q611108|lt=Washinomiya Shrine}} (Kuki, Saitama Prefecture) — Considered the origin of the Great Cock Festival and hosts a smaller rake market * {{ill|Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|ja|熊野神社 (前橋市千代田町)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumano Shrine (Maebashi)|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Maebashi, Gunma Prefecture) — Hosts the Maebashi Great Cock Festival, one of Maebashi's four major festivals * {{ill|Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|ja|金刀比羅・大鷲神社|1=Konpira and Ōtori Shrine|2=ja|3=金刀比羅・大鷲神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kotohira Ōtori Shrine|13=User:Immanuelle/Konpira and Ōtori Shrine|qq=}} (Yokohama, Kanagawa Prefecture) — Its Cock Festival is recognized as an intangible cultural property of Yokohama
Although the {{ill|Ōtori taisha|ja|大鳥神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori taisha|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大鳥大社}} in Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, is regarded as the head shrine of Ōtori faith, its "酉の日祭" (Cock Day Festival), held on the Cock Days in November,<ref>[http://www.ootoritaisha.jp/gyouji/ Ōtori Shrine official website]</ref> does not feature the rake markets or nighttime stalls typical of the Kantō region.
==Origin== The origin of the Cock Festival is explained differently by {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|WD=Q812767|lt=Shinto}} and {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}}.
=== Shinto Explanation === According to Shinto traditions, the Cock Festival originated from markets held on the day of the Great Cock Festival (Ōtori Matsuri). The deities of Ōtori Shrine (or Washi Shrine) include {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|WD=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}}, who prayed for victory during his eastern campaign at {{ill|Washinomiya Shrine|en|Washinomiya Shrine|WD=Q611108|lt=Washinomiya Shrine}}. He later celebrated his victory at the site of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|qq=}} in Hanahata, which also commemorates the day of Yamato Takeru’s death. On November Cock Days (or December’s first Cock Day at Washinomiya Shrine), the Great Cock Festival is held. The shrine tradition of {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} in Asakusa states that Yamato Takeru returned to give thanks on a November Cock Day and leaned his weapons against a pine tree in front of the shrine. This act led to the establishment of the Great Cock Festival and the use of decorative {{ill|Rake (tool)|en|Rake (tool)|WD=Q200822|lt=rakes}} as auspicious items.
=== Buddhist Explanation === In Buddhist tradition, specifically at {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}} in Asakusa, the Cock Festival originates from the market held during the unveiling (kaichō) of the {{ill|Myōken|lt=Washi Myōken Daibosatsu|ja|鷲妙見大菩薩|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōken|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. On a November Cock Day in 1265 (Bun’ei 2), {{ill|Nichiren|ja|Nichiren|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nichiren|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the founder of {{ill|Nichiren Buddhism|ja|Nichiren宗|1=Nichiren Shū|2=ja|3=日蓮宗|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nichiren Buddhism|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q206611}}, was staying at the Kobayakawa household in {{ill|Kazusa Province|en|Kazusa Province|WD=Q1055394|lt=Kazusa Province}} (present-day Mobara City, Chiba Prefecture). While praying for national peace, the morning star (Venus) shone brightly, and Washi Myōken Daibosatsu appeared riding on the back of an eagle. Since the establishment of Chōkoku-ji, the temple has held an annual market on November Cock Days, featuring the transfer of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu from Washiyama-dera. In 1771 (Meiwa 8), the statue of Washi Myōken Daibosatsu was enshrined permanently at Chōkoku-ji, where the annual Cock Festival continued.
=== Historical Practices === The festival is thought to have started as a harvest celebration by nearby farmers at the Hanahata Washi Daimyōjin shrine. Known also as the Rooster Daimyōjin, worshippers abstained from eating chicken meat, and even shrine families refrained from consuming eggs. Farmers offered live chickens as tributes, releasing them at the Asakusa Kannon Hall ({{ill|Sensō-ji|en|Sensō-ji|WD=Q615183|lt=Sensō-ji}}) after the festival.
Because the shrine was conveniently located along the Ayase River, it became a hub for people and goods transported via waterways. As a result, the Cock Day markets gradually attracted visitors from all over Edo (Tokyo). Gambling flourished at these markets until bans during the An’ei era curtailed the festivities.
Eventually, the thriving Cock Festival shifted to the Asakusa Washi Daimyōjin, which became the most prominent venue. Its proximity to {{ill|Yoshiwara|en|Yoshiwara|WD=Q1859550|lt=Yoshiwara}}, a famous red-light district, further contributed to its popularity. Over time, Cock Festivals spread across Edo and are now celebrated at many shrines and temples in the Kantō region.
Thus, the Cock Festival evolved from a rural agricultural market showcasing autumn harvests and farming tools into an urban celebration featuring auspicious decorative rakes symbolizing good fortune and prosperity.
==Customs== [[File:酉の市Torinoichi002.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The Cock Festival at {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|ja|大鷲神社 (足立区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Adachi)|qq=}}. The shrine distributes auspicious {{ill|Rake (tool)|en|Rake (tool)|WD=Q200822|lt=rakes}}.]]
=== Rake Talismans and Decorative Rakes === On the days of the Cock Festival, stalls line up selling "decorative rakes" (engimono kumade), adorned with items such as okame masks and other symbols of good fortune. Shrines hosting the festival also distribute small bamboo {{ill|Rake (tool)|en|Rake (tool)|WD=Q200822|lt=rakes}}, adorned with rice ears and talismans, as "rake talismans" (kumade mamori). These rakes are colloquially called "kakkome," a pun meaning to "sweep in" or "gather in" blessings. Originally, rakes and {{ill|Hoe (tool)|en|Hoe (tool)|WD=Q131154|lt=hoes}}, along with other farming tools, were sold to local farmers around Washi Shrine on festival days. Over time, auspicious items such as okame masks began to be attached to the tools as complimentary gifts, evolving into today's decorative rakes.<ref>[http://www.torinoichi.jp/goriyaku/goriyaku_5.html Cock Festival Benefits]</ref>
The Cock Festival's auspicious items have included "tou no imo" (唐の芋, a type of yam) and "kogane mochi" (黄金餅, millet cakes), since the Edo period. The yam symbolized advancement and promotion due to its "head" shape, while its numerous offspring represented fertility. The millet cakes were believed to bring wealth. However, from the late Edo period, {{ill|kirizansho|ja|切り山椒|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/kirizansho|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 切山椒}}, a type of sweet confection, replaced the millet cakes as a festival item. Eating kirizansho during this cold season is said to prevent colds.<ref>[http://www.otorisama.or.jp/mame.html About the Cock Festival]</ref>
The decorative rake is the festival's iconic auspicious item, symbolizing the talons of an {{ill|Eagle|en|Eagle|WD=Q2092297|lt=eagle}}, which "grasp" its prey. The rake thus conveys the idea of gathering fortune or seizing prosperity. Decorative rakes are often bought through lively bargaining exchanges between rake sellers and buyers, where victorious negotiations are celebrated with exuberant {{ill|Tejime|en|Tejime|WD=Q3982616|lt=tejime}} hand clapping. The size of the decorative rakes tends to grow larger every year, reflecting sellers’ strategies and buyers’ desires for increasing fortune.
=== The Third Cock Day === The "Cock Day" (Tori no Hi) is determined using the {{ill|Sexagenary cycle|en|Sexagenary cycle|WD=Q246658|lt=sexagenary cycle}}, occurring every twelve days.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/learning/elib/qa/qa_35.html |title=Is a Year with Three Cock Days More Prone to Fires? |access-date=2024-12-01 |publisher=Tokyo Fire Department}}</ref> Depending on the month’s alignment, November may have two or three Cock Days.<ref>For instance, if November 3 is the first Cock Day (Ichinotori), then November 15 will be the second (Ninotori), and November 27 the third (Sannotori). However, if November 8 is the first Cock Day, the second falls on November 20, and the next Cock Day occurs in December.</ref> The first Cock Day is called "Ichinotori," the second "Ninotori," and the third "Sannotori."
Years with three Cock Days are traditionally believed to have a higher incidence of fires, though there is no scientific basis for this claim.<ref name=":0" /> Consequently, in years with three Cock Days, greater care is taken with fire safety, especially in late December. Many rake merchants affix "Fire Safety" seals to their rakes during these years. Since three Cock Days occur approximately every other year, they are not particularly rare (see [[#List of Cock Days in November|List of Cock Days in November]]).
In Asakusa's {{ill|Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|ja|鷲神社 (台東区)|1=Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|lt=Ōtori Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taitō)|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōtori Shrine (Taito Ward)|qq=}} and {{ill|Chōkoku-ji|ja|長国寺 (台東区)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkoku-ji|qq=}}, a nearby {{ill|Yoshiwara|en|Yoshiwara|WD=Q1859550|lt=red-light district}} called {{ill|Yoshiwara|en|Yoshiwara|WD=Q1859550|lt=Yoshiwara}} contributed to a peculiar custom. It is said that wives would warn their husbands about the fire risk of the third Cock Day to prevent them from visiting Yoshiwara under the pretense of attending the festival.<ref>[http://ii-nippon.net/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AE%E7%A5%AD/891.html Japanese Festivals: Three Popular Theories]</ref>
